Linear Regression

Topics

Model Assumptions

Classical Linear Regression Assumptions

Let \(n\) be the number of observations and \(p\) the number of predictors, excluding the intercept. With an intercept, there are \(p+1\) coefficients. The population model is

\[y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_{i1}+\cdots+\beta_px_{ip}+\varepsilon_i,\qquad \mathbf y=X\boldsymbol\beta+\boldsymbol\varepsilon.\]

Here \(X\in\mathbb R^{n\times(p+1)}\) is the design matrix, \(\boldsymbol\beta\in\mathbb R^{p+1}\) contains the unknown but fixed coefficients, and \(\boldsymbol\varepsilon\in\mathbb R^n\) is the vector of unobserved errors.

AssumptionMathematical form / meaning
1. Linearity in parameters\(\mathbf y=X\boldsymbol\beta+\boldsymbol\varepsilon\)
The coefficients enter linearly; predictors may be transformed.
2. Random samplingThe observations \((\mathbf x_i,y_i)\) are obtained through random sampling from the population of interest.
3. No perfect multicollinearity\(\operatorname{rank}(X)=p+1=\operatorname{rank}(X^{\mathsf T}X)\)
No column is an exact linear combination of the other columns. The Gram matrix \(X^{\mathsf T}X\) is invertible.
4. ExogeneityZero conditional mean: \(\mathbb E[\boldsymbol\varepsilon\mid X]=\mathbf 0\)
5. Homoskedasticity and uncorrelated errors5a. Constant conditional variance: \(\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_i\mid X)=\sigma_{\varepsilon}^2\) for all \(i\), with \(0<\sigma_{\varepsilon}^2<\infty\).
5b. No correlation between errors: \(\operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon_i,\varepsilon_j\mid X)=0\) for \(i\ne j\).
Together: \(\operatorname{Cov}(\boldsymbol\varepsilon\mid X)=\sigma_{\varepsilon}^2 I_n\) (spherical errors).

Gauss–Markov Theorem

For the linear model, if \(X\) has full column rank and the errors have zero conditional mean and spherical conditional covariance,

\[\mathbb E[\boldsymbol\varepsilon\mid X]=\mathbf0,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(\boldsymbol\varepsilon\mid X)=\sigma_{\varepsilon}^2 I_n,\]

then the Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) estimator

\[\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{\mathrm{OLS}}=(X^{\mathsf T}X)^{-1}X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf y\]
Best Linear Unbiased Estimator (BLUE)

OLS is linear in the observed responses (conditional on \(X\)), unbiased, and has minimum covariance among all linear unbiased estimators of \(\boldsymbol\beta\). In particular, for any fixed vector \(a\),

\[\operatorname{Var}(a^{\mathsf T}\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{\mathrm{OLS}}\mid X)\leq\operatorname{Var}(a^{\mathsf T}\widetilde{\boldsymbol\beta}\mid X).\]

Here \(\widetilde{\boldsymbol\beta}\) is any estimator that is linear in \(\mathbf y\) and conditionally unbiased.

Conclusions from the Assumptions

Under the first four assumptions (GMT 1–4)

  • Unbiasedness: OLS delivers unbiased estimates of the intercept and slopes, \(\mathbb E[\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}\mid X]=\boldsymbol\beta\).
  • Variable inclusion and omission: including an irrelevant variable does not bias the intercept or slope estimates if exogeneity and full rank are maintained, but can increase their variance. Omitting a relevant variable can bias the slope estimates if it is correlated with the included predictors (and may also shift the intercept).

    Consider the true model \(y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_{i1}+\beta_2x_{i2}+\varepsilon_i\). If we regress \(y\) only on \(x_1\) with an intercept, under exogeneity in the true model,

    \[\begin{aligned}\mathbb E[\hat\beta_{1,\mathrm{short}}\mid X_1,X_2]&=\beta_1+\beta_2\delta,\\ \delta&=\frac{\sum_i(x_{i1}-\bar x_1)(x_{i2}-\bar x_2)}{\sum_i(x_{i1}-\bar x_1)^2}.\end{aligned}\]

    Here \(\delta\) is the slope from regressing the omitted predictor \(X_2\) on \(X_1\) with an intercept. Equivalently, using centered predictor vectors, \(\delta=(X_1^TX_1)^{-1}X_1^TX_2\).

    Omitted variable bias: \(\beta_2\delta\). If the omitted variable's effect on \(y\) and its correlation with \(X_1\) have the same sign, the bias is upward; if they have opposite signs, the bias is downward. If either is zero, there is no conditional slope bias in this two-predictor case.

    Financial example: regressing stock returns on market returns without controlling for a relevant size-factor return can bias the estimated market beta if the size factor is correlated with market returns and affects the stock's returns.

  • Consistency: under standard regularity conditions, OLS estimates converge in probability to the true parameter values as the sample size increases, \(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}\xrightarrow{p}\boldsymbol\beta\), and their standard errors tend to zero under the usual finite-variance conditions.

Adding the fifth assumption (GMT 1–5)

  • Efficiency: OLS is the best linear unbiased estimator (BLUE). Best means that it has the lowest variance, and therefore the lowest standard error, among linear unbiased estimators of each coefficient or linear combination of coefficients. This is particularly valuable for inference.
  • Prediction: if the goal is prediction rather than inference, other estimators can trade some bias for lower variance and achieve better out-of-sample performance in many settings (e.g. regularized regression such as Ridge or Lasso).
  • Normality (additional assumption): assumptions 4 and 5 give zero conditional mean and covariance \(\sigma_{\varepsilon}^2 I_n\). If we additionally assume jointly Gaussian errors, then \(\boldsymbol\varepsilon\mid X\sim\mathcal N_n(\mathbf 0,\sigma_{\varepsilon}^2 I_n)\), or equivalently \(\varepsilon_i\mid X\overset{\mathrm{i.i.d.}}{\sim}\mathcal N(0,\sigma_{\varepsilon}^2)\). Normality is not implied by assumptions 4 and 5 and is not required for BLUE, but enables exact classical finite-sample \(t\)- and \(F\)-tests (when \(n>p+1\)).

Assumption Details

1. Linearity in Parameters

The specified model should describe the conditional mean adequately: \(\mathbb E[y_i\mid X]=(X\boldsymbol\beta)_i\) when exogeneity holds.

Why it is needed
A misspecified functional form leaves systematic structure unexplained and can produce biased predictions.
How to validate
Plot residuals vs. fitted values and individual predictors: look for curvature or systematic patterns. Ramsey RESET for a formal check.
Potential remedies
Add polynomial terms, interactions, splines or predictor transformations (e.g. \(\log x\)).

2. Random Sampling

Why it is needed
Random sampling supports generalization. If this assumption is violated, inference may not generalize to the population, and predictions may suffer from large errors.
How to validate
Check the sampling design for selection bias and compare the sample with the target population.
Potential remedies
Improve the sampling design or use justified sampling weights.

3. No Perfect Multicollinearity

Multicollinearity occurs when two or more predictors exhibit strong linear dependence. Perfect multicollinearity occurs when one predictor is an exact linear combination of the others.

\[\operatorname{rank}(X)=p+1=\operatorname{rank}(X^{\mathsf T}X)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad X^{\mathsf T}X\text{ is invertible}.\]
Why it is needed
Perfect multicollinearity prevents unique estimation of the coefficients. Under spherical errors with positive variance, full column rank also guarantees that the coefficient covariance matrix \(\operatorname{Cov}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{\mathrm{OLS}}\mid X)=\sigma_{\varepsilon}^2(X^{\mathsf T}X)^{-1}\) is invertible. High (but not perfect) multicollinearity does not itself bias OLS, but:
  • It is difficult to isolate the individual effects of predictors on the outcome.
  • Individual p-values may be high even for important predictors.
  • Inflated standard errors lead to wide confidence intervals that may include zero, and unstable coefficient estimates.
How to validate
Check the rank of \(X\), inspect the predictor correlation matrix, and calculate VIFs and the condition number to detect near multicollinearity.

Variance inflation factor

\[\operatorname{VIF}_j=\frac{1}{1-R_j^2}\]

Here \(R_j^2\) comes from regressing predictor \(j\) on the other predictors (including an intercept in the auxiliary regression). A VIF above 5 is a common warning heuristic, not a universal statistical threshold.

Potential remedies
Evaluate correlation between predictors and select one per family group, consider PCA or regularization

4. Exogeneity

Zero conditional mean (absence of endogeneity)

\[\mathbb E[\boldsymbol\varepsilon\mid X]=\mathbf0\]
Why it is needed
Ensures conditional unbiasedness of OLS.

Derivation: unbiasedness of OLS

Substitute the model \(y=X\boldsymbol\beta+\boldsymbol\varepsilon\) into the OLS estimator:

\[\begin{aligned} \widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}&=(X^{\mathsf T}X)^{-1}X^{\mathsf T}y\\ &=\boldsymbol\beta+(X^{\mathsf T}X)^{-1}X^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\varepsilon. \end{aligned}\]

Taking the expectation conditional on \(X\):

\[\begin{aligned} \mathbb E[\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}\mid X] &=\boldsymbol\beta+(X^{\mathsf T}X)^{-1}X^{\mathsf T}\mathbb E[\boldsymbol\varepsilon\mid X]\\ &=\boldsymbol\beta. \end{aligned}\]
How to validate
Plot residuals vs. individual predictors to look for systematic nonlinear patterns. Check for omitted confounders, reverse causality and measurement error. Use Durbin-Wu-Hausman to check for consistency

Why residual plots cannot establish exogeneity

The OLS normal equations imply

\[\begin{aligned} X^{\mathsf T}\widehat{\boldsymbol\varepsilon} &=X^{\mathsf T}(y-X\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta})\\ &=X^{\mathsf T}y-X^{\mathsf T}X(X^{\mathsf T}X)^{-1}X^{\mathsf T}y\\ &=\mathbf0. \end{aligned}\]

With an intercept, the sample correlation between every nonconstant included predictor and the nonconstant OLS residuals is zero by construction. Residual plots can flag model misspecification, but a clean plot does not establish \(\mathbb E[\boldsymbol\varepsilon\mid X]=\mathbf0\).

Potential remedies
Include relevant confounders and improve measurements

5. Homoskedasticity and Uncorrelated Errors

5a. Homoskedasticity

\[\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_i\mid X)=\sigma_{\varepsilon}^2\]

Together with assumption 5b (uncorrelated errors), this gives the spherical conditional covariance matrix of the errors:

\[\operatorname{Cov}(\boldsymbol\varepsilon\mid X)=\sigma_{\varepsilon}^2 I_n=\begin{pmatrix}\sigma_{\varepsilon}^2&0&\cdots&0\\0&\sigma_{\varepsilon}^2&\cdots&0\\\vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\0&0&\cdots&\sigma_{\varepsilon}^2\end{pmatrix}.\]
Why it is needed
With heteroskedasticity, the conventional OLS variance estimator uses a single pooled estimate of the error variance instead of accounting for its variation across observations. OLS coefficient estimates remain unbiased if exogeneity holds, but can be less precise than those of an appropriately weighted estimator. Conventional standard errors may be biased, leading to misleading hypothesis tests, p-values and confidence intervals.

Derivation: covariance of the OLS estimator

From the estimator decomposition in assumption 4, with \(A=(X^{\mathsf T}X)^{-1}X^{\mathsf T}\):

\[\begin{aligned} \operatorname{Cov}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}\mid X) &=A\operatorname{Cov}(\boldsymbol\varepsilon\mid X)A^{\mathsf T}\\ &=(X^{\mathsf T}X)^{-1}X^{\mathsf T}\operatorname{Cov}(\boldsymbol\varepsilon\mid X)X(X^{\mathsf T}X)^{-1}. \end{aligned}\]

Under assumptions 5a and 5b, \(\operatorname{Cov}(\boldsymbol\varepsilon\mid X)=\sigma_{\varepsilon}^2 I_n\), so

\[\begin{aligned} \operatorname{Cov}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}\mid X) &=\sigma_{\varepsilon}^2(X^{\mathsf T}X)^{-1}X^{\mathsf T}X(X^{\mathsf T}X)^{-1}\\ &=\sigma_{\varepsilon}^2(X^{\mathsf T}X)^{-1}. \end{aligned}\]

If homoskedasticity or error uncorrelatedness fails, this simplification is generally invalid, but the unbiasedness result from assumption 4 still holds. Under Gauss–Markov, OLS has minimum covariance among linear unbiased estimators.

How to validate
Plot residuals vs. fitted values: look for a fanning effect (funnel shape or changing spread), indicating heteroskedasticity. Use the Breusch–Pagan or White test.
Potential remedies
Refit using a concave transformation of the response (e.g. \(\log y\) for positive responses, when appropriate), or use weighted least squares with weights \(w_i\propto 1/\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_i\mid X)\) when the error variances can be estimated. For inference with independent observations, consider heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors (e.g. HC3).

5b. No correlation between error terms

\[\operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon_i,\varepsilon_j\mid X)=0,\qquad i\ne j.\]
Why it is needed
If errors are correlated (e.g. in time-series data), OLS estimates remain unbiased provided exogeneity holds, but conventional standard errors can be biased, often downward when errors are positively correlated. This can lead to overly narrow confidence intervals and misleadingly small p-values, resulting in incorrect inference. OLS may also lose efficiency.

Example

Duplicating the same dataset increases the apparent sample size from \(n\) to \(2n\) without adding any information. The OLS coefficient estimates remain unchanged, but conventional coefficient standard errors decrease by approximately a factor of \(\sqrt{2}\), creating a false impression of greater precision.

How to validate
Plot residuals in time or group order; inspect the ACF for serial correlation and within-group dependence. Use Durbin–Watson or Breusch–Godfrey where applicable.
Potential remedies
Use HAC / Newey–West or cluster-robust standard errors; consider GLS or explicitly model the dependence.

Multiple Linear Regression

Model and Dimensions

Let \(n\) be the number of observations and \(p\) the number of predictors, excluding the intercept. With an intercept, there are \(p+1\) coefficients. For observation \(i\), the population model is

\[y_i=\beta_0+\sum_{j=1}^{p}\beta_j x_{ij}+\varepsilon_i.\]

In matrix notation, with the first column of \(X\) equal to one:

\[\mathbf y=X\boldsymbol\beta+\boldsymbol\varepsilon,\qquad \widehat{\mathbf y}=X\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta},\qquad \mathbf e=\mathbf y-\widehat{\mathbf y}.\]
ObjectDimensionsMeaning
\(\mathbf y\)\(n\times1\)Observed response vector
\(X\)\(n\times(p+1)\)Design matrix: \(n\) observations and \(p+1\) columns: \(p\) predictors and the intercept column
\(\boldsymbol\beta\)\((p+1)\times1\)Unknown population coefficients
\(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}\)\((p+1)\times1\)Estimated model coefficients
\(\boldsymbol\varepsilon\)\(n\times1\)Unobserved population error terms
\(\widehat{\mathbf y}\)\(n\times1\)Fitted response vector
\(\mathbf e\)\(n\times1\)Observed in-sample residuals after fitting

Matrix construction (intercept included)

\[ \underbrace{\begin{pmatrix}y_1\\y_2\\\vdots\\y_n\end{pmatrix}}_{n\times1} =\underbrace{\begin{pmatrix}1&x_{11}&\cdots&x_{1,p}\\1&x_{21}&\cdots&x_{2,p}\\\vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\1&x_{n1}&\cdots&x_{n,p}\end{pmatrix}}_{n\times(p+1)} \underbrace{\begin{pmatrix}\beta_0\\\beta_1\\\vdots\\\beta_{p}\end{pmatrix}}_{(p+1)\times1} +\underbrace{\begin{pmatrix}\varepsilon_1\\\varepsilon_2\\\vdots\\\varepsilon_n\end{pmatrix}}_{n\times1}. \]

Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) Objective

Ordinary least squares chooses the coefficients that minimize the sum of squared differences between observed and fitted responses. Let \(\mathbf x_i^T\) be row \(i\) of \(X\), including the intercept.

\[\operatorname{RSS}(\boldsymbol\beta)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i-\mathbf x_i^T\boldsymbol\beta)^2=\lVert\mathbf y-X\boldsymbol\beta\rVert_2^2.\]
\[\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}=\underset{\boldsymbol\beta\in\mathbb R^{p+1}}{\operatorname{argmin}}\;\operatorname{RSS}(\boldsymbol\beta).\]

Expand the RSS

\[\begin{aligned} \operatorname{RSS}(\boldsymbol\beta)&=(\mathbf y-X\boldsymbol\beta)^T(\mathbf y-X\boldsymbol\beta)\\ &=(\mathbf y^T-\boldsymbol\beta^TX^T)(\mathbf y-X\boldsymbol\beta)\\ &=\mathbf y^T\mathbf y-\mathbf y^TX\boldsymbol\beta-\boldsymbol\beta^TX^T\mathbf y+\boldsymbol\beta^TX^TX\boldsymbol\beta\\ &=\mathbf y^T\mathbf y-2\boldsymbol\beta^TX^T\mathbf y+\boldsymbol\beta^TX^TX\boldsymbol\beta. \end{aligned}\]

The two cross-terms are equal because \(\mathbf y^TX\boldsymbol\beta\) is a scalar and equals its transpose \(\boldsymbol\beta^TX^T\mathbf y\).

Derive the Gradient of RSS

Differentiate each term with respect to the coefficient vector \(\boldsymbol\beta\), treating \(X\) and \(\mathbf y\) as fixed. For a scalar-valued function \(f\), the gradient is defined by its differential:

\[df=(\nabla_{\boldsymbol\beta}f)^T d\boldsymbol\beta.\]

1. Constant term

\[d(\mathbf y^T\mathbf y)=0,\qquad\nabla_{\boldsymbol\beta}(\mathbf y^T\mathbf y)=\mathbf 0.\]

The response vector does not depend on the coefficient vector.

2. Linear term

\[\begin{aligned} f(\boldsymbol\beta)&=-2\boldsymbol\beta^TX^T\mathbf y,\\ f(\boldsymbol\beta+d\boldsymbol\beta)&=-2(\boldsymbol\beta+d\boldsymbol\beta)^TX^T\mathbf y\\ &=-2\boldsymbol\beta^TX^T\mathbf y-2(d\boldsymbol\beta)^TX^T\mathbf y,\\ df&=-2(d\boldsymbol\beta)^TX^T\mathbf y\\ &=(-2X^T\mathbf y)^T d\boldsymbol\beta,\\ \therefore\quad\nabla_{\boldsymbol\beta}f&=-2X^T\mathbf y. \end{aligned}\]

3. Quadratic term

Let \(A=X^TX\). Since \(A^T=A\),

\[\begin{aligned} f(\boldsymbol\beta)&=\boldsymbol\beta^TA\boldsymbol\beta,\\ f(\boldsymbol\beta+d\boldsymbol\beta)&=(\boldsymbol\beta+d\boldsymbol\beta)^TA(\boldsymbol\beta+d\boldsymbol\beta)\\ &=\boldsymbol\beta^TA\boldsymbol\beta+\boldsymbol\beta^TA\,d\boldsymbol\beta\\ &\quad+(d\boldsymbol\beta)^TA\boldsymbol\beta+(d\boldsymbol\beta)^TA\,d\boldsymbol\beta. \end{aligned}\]

The last term is second order in \(d\boldsymbol\beta\), so it does not contribute to the first-order differential. The other two increment terms are equal because \(A\) is symmetric.

\[\begin{aligned} df&=\boldsymbol\beta^TA\,d\boldsymbol\beta+(d\boldsymbol\beta)^TA\boldsymbol\beta\\ &=(A^T\boldsymbol\beta)^T d\boldsymbol\beta+(A\boldsymbol\beta)^T d\boldsymbol\beta\\ &=((A+A^T)\boldsymbol\beta)^T d\boldsymbol\beta\\ &=(2A\boldsymbol\beta)^T d\boldsymbol\beta,\\ \therefore\quad\nabla_{\boldsymbol\beta}f&=2A\boldsymbol\beta=2X^TX\boldsymbol\beta. \end{aligned}\]
RSS gradient
\[\nabla_{\boldsymbol\beta}\operatorname{RSS}(\boldsymbol\beta)=-2X^T\mathbf y+2X^TX\boldsymbol\beta=-2X^T(\mathbf y-X\boldsymbol\beta).\]

Derive the OLS Coefficients

Set the gradient to zero at the stationary point:

\[\begin{aligned} -2X^T(\mathbf y-X\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta})&=\mathbf0\\ X^T\mathbf y-X^TX\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}&=\mathbf0\\ X^TX\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}&=X^T\mathbf y. \end{aligned}\]

These are the normal equations.

Solve the normal equations

If the columns of \(X\) are linearly independent, \(X^TX\) is invertible. Multiply both sides by its inverse:

\[\begin{aligned} (X^TX)^{-1}X^TX\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}&=(X^TX)^{-1}X^T\mathbf y\\ I_{p+1}\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}&=(X^TX)^{-1}X^T\mathbf y. \end{aligned}\]
OLS estimator
\[\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}=(X^TX)^{-1}X^T\mathbf y.\]

Why is the stationary point a minimum?

Differentiate the gradient again to obtain the Hessian:

\[H=\nabla_{\boldsymbol\beta}^{2}\operatorname{RSS}(\boldsymbol\beta)=2X^TX.\]

For any nonzero \(\mathbf v\in\mathbb R^{p+1}\),

\[\begin{aligned} \mathbf v^TH\mathbf v&=2\mathbf v^TX^TX\mathbf v\\ &=2(X\mathbf v)^T(X\mathbf v)\\ &=2\lVert X\mathbf v\rVert_2^2\geq0. \end{aligned}\]

The Hessian is positive semidefinite, so RSS is convex and every stationary point is a global minimum. The inequality is strict for every nonzero \(\mathbf v\) exactly when \(X\) has full column rank. In this case the Hessian is positive definite, RSS is strictly convex, and the coefficient solution is unique.

Geometric Interpretation

The fitted vector \(\widehat{\mathbf y}=X\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}\) lies in the column space of \(X\). Least squares chooses the closest vector in that subspace to \(\mathbf y\). The residual is orthogonal to every column of \(X\).

Orthogonality and the projection matrix

From the normal equations,

\[\begin{aligned} X^TX\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}&=X^T\mathbf y\\ X^T(\mathbf y-X\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta})&=\mathbf0\\ X^T\mathbf e&=\mathbf0. \end{aligned}\]

For full-column-rank \(X\), substitute the coefficient formula into \(\widehat{\mathbf y}=X\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}\):

\[\begin{aligned} \widehat{\mathbf y}&=X(X^TX)^{-1}X^T\mathbf y\\ &=P_X\mathbf y,\\ P_X&=X(X^TX)^{-1}X^T,\\ \mathbf e&=\mathbf y-P_X\mathbf y=(I_n-P_X)\mathbf y. \end{aligned}\]

\(P_X\) is the orthogonal projector onto \(\operatorname{col}(X)\), also known as the hat matrix. It is symmetric and idempotent: \(P_X^T=P_X\) and \(P_X^2=P_X\).

Projection and residuals
\[\widehat{\mathbf y}=P_X\mathbf y,\qquad \mathbf e=(I_n-P_X)\mathbf y,\qquad X^T\mathbf e=\mathbf0.\]

Simple Linear Regression

Model and Formalism

Simple linear regression models the relationship between a single predictor \(X\) and a response \(Y\) using a straight line. The population model and its fitted counterpart are

\[Y=\beta_0+\beta_1 X+\varepsilon,\qquad \hat y_i=\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1 x_i.\]
TermInterpretation
Intercept \(\beta_0\)Expected response when \(X=0\): \(E[Y\mid X=0]=\beta_0\), under the zero conditional mean assumption. Its practical interpretation depends on whether zero is meaningful for the predictor.
Slope \(\beta_1\)Change in the expected response associated with a one-unit increase in \(X\).
Error \(\varepsilon_i\)Unobserved difference between the observed response and the population regression line.
Residual \(e_i\)Observed difference between the response and the estimated regression line: \(e_i=y_i-\hat y_i\).

The population coefficients are unknown; they are estimated using the observed sample. Under the assumptions for unbiasedness, repeated sampling gives \(E[\hat\beta_j\mid X]=\beta_j\) for \(j=0,1\).

Least Squares Objective

Given the observed pairs \((x_i,y_i)\), choose the intercept and slope that minimize the sum of squared residuals.

\[\operatorname{RSS}(\beta_0,\beta_1)=\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-\beta_0-\beta_1x_i)^2.\]
\[(\hat\beta_0,\hat\beta_1)=\underset{\beta_0,\beta_1}{\operatorname{argmin}}\;\operatorname{RSS}(\beta_0,\beta_1).\]

Derive the OLS Coefficients

Differentiate RSS with respect to both coefficients and set the derivatives equal to zero. Define the sample means

\[\bar x=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n x_i,\qquad \bar y=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n y_i.\]

1. Partial derivative with respect to the intercept

\[\begin{aligned} 0&=\left.\frac{\partial\operatorname{RSS}}{\partial\beta_0}\right|_{\hat\beta_0,\hat\beta_1}\\ &=\sum_{i=1}^n 2(y_i-\hat\beta_0-\hat\beta_1 x_i)(-1)\\ &=-2\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-\hat\beta_0-\hat\beta_1 x_i),\\ 0&=\sum_{i=1}^n y_i-n\hat\beta_0-\hat\beta_1\sum_{i=1}^n x_i,\\ n\hat\beta_0&=\sum_{i=1}^n y_i-\hat\beta_1\sum_{i=1}^n x_i,\\ \hat\beta_0&=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n y_i-\hat\beta_1\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\\ &=\bar y-\hat\beta_1\bar x. \end{aligned}\]

The intercept estimator depends on the slope estimator.

2. Partial derivative with respect to the slope

\[\begin{aligned} 0&=\left.\frac{\partial\operatorname{RSS}}{\partial\beta_1}\right|_{\hat\beta_0,\hat\beta_1}\\ &=\sum_{i=1}^n 2(y_i-\hat\beta_0-\hat\beta_1 x_i)(-x_i)\\ &=-2\sum_{i=1}^n x_i(y_i-\hat\beta_0-\hat\beta_1 x_i),\\ 0&=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i y_i-\hat\beta_0\sum_{i=1}^n x_i-\hat\beta_1\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2. \end{aligned}\]

Substitute the intercept obtained above:

\[\begin{aligned} 0&=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i y_i-(\bar y-\hat\beta_1\bar x)\sum_{i=1}^n x_i-\hat\beta_1\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^2\\ &=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i(y_i-\bar y)-\hat\beta_1\sum_{i=1}^n x_i(x_i-\bar x),\\ \hat\beta_1\sum_{i=1}^n x_i(x_i-\bar x)&=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i(y_i-\bar y). \end{aligned}\]

Because the centered observations sum to zero,

\[\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i-n\bar x=0,\qquad\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-\bar y)=0.\]

Rewrite each sum using these identities:

\[\begin{aligned} \sum_{i=1}^n x_i(x_i-\bar x)&=\sum_{i=1}^n\big[(x_i-\bar x)+\bar x\big](x_i-\bar x)\\ &=\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)^2+\bar x\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)\\ &=\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)^2,\\[6pt] \sum_{i=1}^n x_i(y_i-\bar y)&=\sum_{i=1}^n\big[(x_i-\bar x)+\bar x\big](y_i-\bar y)\\ &=\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y)+\bar x\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-\bar y)\\ &=\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y). \end{aligned}\]

Therefore,

\[\hat\beta_1\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)^2=\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y).\]
OLS estimators
\[\hat\beta_1=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y)}{\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)^2},\qquad \hat\beta_0=\bar y-\hat\beta_1\bar x.\]

The fitted line passes through \((\bar x,\bar y)\). The solution is unique if the predictor is not constant, by the positive-definite Hessian result in Multiple Linear Regression.

Equivalent Forms of the Slope

Let \(S_{xx}=\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2\), \(S_{xy}=\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y)\), and \(S_{yy}=\sum_i(y_i-\bar y)^2\). Write \(s_x,s_y\) for sample standard deviations and \(s_{xy}\) for sample covariance, using the same denominator \(n-1\).

FormSlope estimator
Centered sums\(\displaystyle\hat\beta_1=\frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}}\)
Only predictor centered\(\displaystyle\hat\beta_1=\frac{\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)y_i}{\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2}\)
Raw-score form\(\displaystyle\hat\beta_1=\frac{\sum_i x_i y_i-n\bar x\bar y}{\sum_i x_i^2-n\bar x^2}\)
Covariance / variance\(\displaystyle\hat\beta_1=\frac{s_{xy}}{s_x^2}\)
Correlation form\(\displaystyle\hat\beta_1=r_{xy}\frac{s_y}{s_x}\) (when both standard deviations are positive)

Derive the alternative forms

\[\begin{aligned} S_{xy}&=\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)y_i-\bar y\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)\\ &=\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)y_i\\ &=\sum_i x_i y_i-n\bar x\bar y,\\ S_{xx}&=\sum_i x_i^2-2\bar x\sum_i x_i+n\bar x^2\\ &=\sum_i x_i^2-n\bar x^2. \end{aligned}\]
\[\hat\beta_1=\frac{S_{xy}/(n-1)}{S_{xx}/(n-1)}=\frac{s_{xy}}{s_x^2}.\]

When \(s_y>0\), Pearson correlation is

\[r_{xy}=\frac{S_{xy}}{\sqrt{S_{xx}S_{yy}}}=\frac{s_{xy}}{s_xs_y}.\]
\[\hat\beta_1=\frac{s_{xy}}{s_x^2}=\frac{s_{xy}}{s_xs_y}\frac{s_y}{s_x}=r_{xy}\frac{s_y}{s_x},\qquad r_{xy}=\hat\beta_1\frac{s_x}{s_y}.\]

Centering the Variables

Let \(\tilde x_i=x_i-\bar x\) and \(\tilde y_i=y_i-\bar y\). Translating the predictor or response does not change the slope.

CoordinatesFitted model
Original\(\hat y_i=\bar y-\hat\beta_1\bar x+\hat\beta_1x_i\)
Center only \(x\)\(\hat y_i=\bar y+\hat\beta_1\tilde x_i\)
Center both \(x,y\)\(\widehat{\tilde y}_i=\hat\beta_1\tilde x_i\)

Why the intercept changes

With centered predictor, the intercept normal equation becomes

\[0=\sum_i y_i-n\hat\alpha-\hat\beta_1\underbrace{\sum_i\tilde x_i}_{0}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\hat\alpha=\bar y.\]

If the response is centered as well, its mean is zero, giving \(\hat\alpha=0\). The slope is unchanged:

\[\hat\beta_1=\frac{\sum_i\tilde x_i\tilde y_i}{\sum_i\tilde x_i^2}=\frac{\sum_i\tilde x_i y_i}{\sum_i\tilde x_i^2}.\]

Centering both variables gives a zero intercept, without changing the slope.

Example: Least Squares Calculations

Fit a simple linear regression to the seven observations below. First center the predictor, then compute the slope using the centered values.

\[\bar x=\frac{2800}{7}=400,\qquad\bar y=\frac{420}{7}=60,\qquad\tilde x_i=x_i-400.\]
\(x_i\)\(y_i\)\(\tilde x_i\)\(y_i\tilde x_i\)\(\tilde x_i^2\)\(\hat y_i\)\(e_i\)\(e_i^2\)
10040-300-12,00090,00039.640.360.13
20045-200-9,00040,00046.43-1.432.04
30050-100-5,00010,00053.21-3.2110.33
4006500060.005.0025.00
500701007,00010,00066.793.2110.33
6007020014,00040,00073.57-3.5712.76
7008030024,00090,00080.36-0.360.13
2,800420019,000280,000420.000.0060.71

Calculate the coefficients

\[\begin{aligned} \hat\beta_1&=\frac{\sum_i y_i\tilde x_i}{\sum_i\tilde x_i^2}=\frac{19000}{280000}=\frac{19}{280}\approx0.067857,\\ \hat\beta_0&=\bar y-\hat\beta_1\bar x=60-\frac{19}{280}(400)=\frac{230}{7}\approx32.8571. \end{aligned}\]

Using the centered predictor, the fitted line is \(\hat y=60+\frac{19}{280}\tilde x\). In the original coordinates,

\[\hat y=60+\frac{19}{280}(x-400)=\frac{230}{7}+\frac{19}{280}x.\]
Fitted regression line
\[\hat y\approx32.8571+0.067857x.\]

Residual variance and standard error

\[\begin{aligned} \operatorname{RSS}(\hat\beta_0,\hat\beta_1)&=\sum_{i=1}^7 e_i^2=\frac{425}{7}\approx60.7143,\\ \hat\sigma_\varepsilon^2&=\frac{\operatorname{RSS}}{n-2}=\frac{425/7}{5}=\frac{85}{7}\approx12.1429,\\ \hat\sigma_\varepsilon&=\sqrt{\frac{85}{7}}\approx3.48. \end{aligned}\]

With \(p=1\) predictor and an intercept, two coefficients are estimated, leaving \(n-p-1=n-2=5\) residual degrees of freedom. The table uses the unrounded slope for calculations and rounds displayed values only. Using the source's rounded slope \(0.068\) instead gives \(\hat y=32.8+0.068x\) and RSS \(=60.72\).

How to Train

Ordinary Least Squares (OLS)

The method of least squares is the original method that learns the parameters of the hyperplane that best approximates the output from the input data.

\[\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{\mathrm{OLS}}=\underset{\boldsymbol\beta}{\operatorname{argmin}}\;\operatorname{RSS}(\boldsymbol\beta),\qquad \operatorname{RSS}(\boldsymbol\beta)=\lVert\mathbf y-X\boldsymbol\beta\rVert_2^2.\]

When \(X\) has full column rank, the normal equations give the unique solution:

\[\boxed{\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{\mathrm{OLS}}=(X^TX)^{-1}X^T\mathbf y}.\]

See Multiple Linear Regression — RSS gradient and OLS coefficients and Hessian for the full derivations.

In practice, use a numerical least-squares solver (e.g. QR or SVD) instead of explicitly computing the inverse. OLS does not require normally distributed errors.

Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE)

MLE specifies a probability distribution for the observed responses conditional on the predictors and chooses the parameters that maximize the likelihood of the observed data. Assume independent Gaussian errors conditional on \(X\), with mean zero and common variance \(\sigma_\varepsilon^2>0\).

\[\begin{aligned}\boldsymbol\varepsilon\mid X&\sim\mathcal N_n(\mathbf 0,\sigma_\varepsilon^2 I_n),\\ y_i\mid X;\boldsymbol\beta,\sigma_\varepsilon^2&\sim\mathcal N(\mathbf x_i^T\boldsymbol\beta,\sigma_\varepsilon^2).\end{aligned}\]

Derive the likelihood and log-likelihood

For one observation, the conditional density is

\[p(y_i\mid X;\boldsymbol\beta,\sigma_\varepsilon^2)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma_\varepsilon^2}}\exp\!\left[-\frac{(y_i-\mathbf x_i^T\boldsymbol\beta)^2}{2\sigma_\varepsilon^2}\right].\]

Conditional independence allows us to multiply the densities:

\[\begin{aligned}\mathcal L(\boldsymbol\beta,\sigma_\varepsilon^2\mid X,\mathbf y)&=\prod_{i=1}^n p(y_i\mid X;\boldsymbol\beta,\sigma_\varepsilon^2)\\&=(2\pi\sigma_\varepsilon^2)^{-n/2}\exp\!\left[-\frac{1}{2\sigma_\varepsilon^2}\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-\mathbf x_i^T\boldsymbol\beta)^2\right].\end{aligned}\]

Take the logarithm (a monotonically increasing function):

\[\begin{aligned}\ell(\boldsymbol\beta,\sigma_\varepsilon^2)&=\log\mathcal L(\boldsymbol\beta,\sigma_\varepsilon^2\mid X,\mathbf y)\\&=-\frac n2\log(2\pi\sigma_\varepsilon^2)-\frac{\operatorname{RSS}(\boldsymbol\beta)}{2\sigma_\varepsilon^2}.\end{aligned}\]

Maximize with respect to the coefficients

For any fixed positive \(\sigma_\varepsilon^2\), the first term does not depend on \(\boldsymbol\beta\) and the second is a negative multiple of RSS. Thus

\[\underset{\boldsymbol\beta}{\operatorname{argmax}}\;\ell(\boldsymbol\beta,\sigma_\varepsilon^2)=\underset{\boldsymbol\beta}{\operatorname{argmin}}\;\operatorname{RSS}(\boldsymbol\beta).\]

Using the previously derived RSS gradient,

\[\begin{aligned}\nabla_{\boldsymbol\beta}\ell&=-\frac{1}{2\sigma_\varepsilon^2}\nabla_{\boldsymbol\beta}\operatorname{RSS}(\boldsymbol\beta)\\&=\frac{X^T(\mathbf y-X\boldsymbol\beta)}{\sigma_\varepsilon^2}=\mathbf 0\\&\Longrightarrow X^TX\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}=X^T\mathbf y.\end{aligned}\]
\[\boxed{\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{\mathrm{MLE}}=\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{\mathrm{OLS}}=(X^TX)^{-1}X^T\mathbf y}\]

Under the Gaussian model and full column rank, the coefficient estimates are identical. Normality is not needed for OLS or Gauss–Markov; it gives this Gaussian likelihood interpretation and the usual exact finite-sample Gaussian inference.

MLE of the Error Variance

The likelihood also allows us to estimate the error variance. Let \(v=\sigma_\varepsilon^2\).

Maximize with respect to the variance

\[\begin{aligned}\ell(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta},v)&=-\frac n2\log(2\pi v)-\frac{\operatorname{RSS}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta})}{2v},\\\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial v}&=-\frac n{2v}+\frac{\operatorname{RSS}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta})}{2v^2}=0,\\ nv&=\operatorname{RSS}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}),\\\widehat v&=\frac{\operatorname{RSS}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta})}{n}.\end{aligned}\]

For positive RSS, the derivative is positive below this value and negative above it, so this is a maximum.

\[\boxed{\widehat{\sigma}_{\varepsilon,\mathrm{MLE}}^2=\frac{\operatorname{RSS}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta})}{n}},\qquad \boxed{\widehat{\sigma}_{\varepsilon,\mathrm{unbiased}}^2=\frac{\operatorname{RSS}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta})}{n-p-1}}.\]

Unlike the classical unbiased variance estimator, the Gaussian MLE divides by \(n\), not the residual degrees of freedom. Under the classical assumptions, with an intercept, \(E[\operatorname{RSS}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta})\mid X]=(n-p-1)\sigma_\varepsilon^2\). The MLE is therefore biased downward in finite samples. A perfect fit (RSS equal to zero) gives no positive finite variance maximizer.

Throughout these notes, \(p\) counts predictors only, excluding the intercept. For a full-column-rank model with positive residual degrees of freedom:

ModelResidual degrees of freedomUnbiased error variance estimator
With intercept\(n-p-1\)\(\displaystyle\frac{\operatorname{RSS}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta})}{n-p-1}\)
Without intercept\(n-p\)\(\displaystyle\frac{\operatorname{RSS}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta})}{n-p}\)

Gradient Descent

Gradient descent is an iterative optimization algorithm for minimizing a differentiable loss \(L(\boldsymbol\theta)\). The gradient is the vector of partial derivatives and points in the direction of steepest local increase:

\[\nabla_{\boldsymbol\theta}L(\boldsymbol\theta)=\begin{pmatrix}\frac{\partial L}{\partial\theta_1}\\\vdots\\\frac{\partial L}{\partial\theta_d}\end{pmatrix}.\]

Starting from an initial parameter vector \(\boldsymbol\theta_0\), move in the opposite direction of the gradient:

\[\boxed{\boldsymbol\theta_{t+1}=\boldsymbol\theta_t-\eta\nabla_{\boldsymbol\theta}L(\boldsymbol\theta_t)},\qquad \eta>0.\]

The learning rate \(\eta\) controls the step size. A small value can make convergence slow; a large value can cause overshooting or divergence. For a smooth loss, a sufficiently small step decreases the loss when the gradient is nonzero. A convex loss has no nonglobal local minima.

Convergence: local vs global minimum

A local minimum has the lowest loss within its neighborhood; a global minimum has the lowest loss over the entire parameter space. For a convex loss, every local minimum is global. Convexity alone does not guarantee that a minimum is attained or that a particular gradient descent step size will converge.

For a differentiable convex loss with a Lipschitz-continuous gradient and an attained minimum, gradient descent with a sufficiently small fixed learning rate converges in objective value to the global minimum from any starting point. For OLS, the RSS is convex and has a minimum; full column rank makes it strictly convex with a unique solution (see OLS coefficients and Hessian).

For nonconvex losses, gradient descent can converge to a nonglobal local minimum or other stationary point. Initialization and the learning rate matter; a zero gradient alone does not establish global optimality.

Application to linear regression

Using the mean squared error as the loss (which has the same minimizer as RSS),

\[\begin{aligned}L(\boldsymbol\beta)&=\frac1n\lVert\mathbf y-X\boldsymbol\beta\rVert_2^2,\\\nabla_{\boldsymbol\beta}L(\boldsymbol\beta)&=-\frac2nX^T(\mathbf y-X\boldsymbol\beta),\\\boldsymbol\beta_{t+1}&=\boldsymbol\beta_t+\frac{2\eta}{n}X^T(\mathbf y-X\boldsymbol\beta_t).\end{aligned}\]

With full column rank and a suitable learning rate, gradient descent converges to the same coefficients as OLS. Feature scaling often improves convergence. Stop when the gradient norm or the improvement in loss is sufficiently small, or a maximum number of iterations is reached.

Example A — one-dimensional quadratic loss

Take \(L(w)=(w-3)^2\), \(w_0=0\), and \(\eta=0.1\).

\[\begin{aligned}L'(w)&=2(w-3),\\w_{t+1}&=w_t-0.1\cdot2(w_t-3),\\w_1&=0-0.1(-6)=0.6,\\w_2&=0.6-0.1(-4.8)=1.08,\\w_3&=1.08-0.1(-3.84)=1.464.\end{aligned}\]

The minimum is \(w=3\). With this learning rate the iterates approach it without overshooting.

Example B — two-dimensional quadratic loss

Let \(L(x,y)=(x-1)^2+2(y+2)^2\), with \((x_0,y_0)=(4,0)\) and \(\eta=0.1\).

\[\begin{aligned}\nabla L(x,y)&=\begin{pmatrix}2(x-1)\\4(y+2)\end{pmatrix},\\(x_1,y_1)&=(4,0)-0.1(6,8)=(3.4,-0.8),\\(x_2,y_2)&=(3.4,-0.8)-0.1(4.8,4.8)=(2.92,-1.28),\\(x_3,y_3)&=(2.92,-1.28)-0.1(3.84,2.88)=(2.536,-1.568).\end{aligned}\]

Both gradient components are updated simultaneously, and the optimum is \((1,-2)\).

Gradient Descent vs Stochastic Gradient Descent

For a loss that averages individual observation losses, \(L(\boldsymbol\theta)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n L_i(\boldsymbol\theta)\), the full gradient averages all individual gradients. Stochastic and mini-batch gradient descent approximate it using fewer observations per update.

MethodGradient used per updateAdvantages and limitations
Batch GD
All observations		\(\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\nabla L_i\)Exact, deterministic gradient; stable updates with a suitable learning rate. Each update processes the entire dataset.
SGD
One observation		\(\nabla L_{i_t}\)Cheap and frequent updates; useful for large or streaming datasets. Noisy trajectory; may fluctuate near the optimum with a fixed learning rate.
Mini-batch GD
Subset of observations		\(\frac1{|B_t|}\sum_{i\in B_t}\nabla L_i\)Balances gradient noise and computational efficiency; supports vectorization and GPU parallelism. Batch size and learning rate need tuning.

With uniform random sampling, the stochastic gradient is an unbiased estimate of the full gradient at the current parameters. For linear regression with dense data, the gradient costs per update are \(O(n(p+1))\), \(O(p+1)\), and \(O(b(p+1))\) for full batch, SGD, and mini-batch size \(b\), respectively. An epoch corresponds to roughly one pass through the dataset.

Practical choice: for ordinary linear regression of manageable size, a direct least-squares solver is usually preferable. For very large datasets, streaming data or more general differentiable models, iterative methods can avoid forming and factorizing \(X^TX\). Mini-batch GD is often a useful compromise; use feature scaling and a suitable learning rate or schedule.

Goodness of Fit

Total, Explained and Residual Sums of Squares

Goodness-of-fit measures assess how well the fitted model explains the observed variation in the response. They help compare model specifications on the same fitting sample. To assess predictive performance on unseen data, use out-of-sample testing or cross-validation.

To measure the improvement over predicting the sample mean for every observation, split the total variation into the part explained by the regression and the part left in its residuals.

QuantityDefinitionInterpretation
TSS — Total\(\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-\bar y)^2\)Total observed variation around the sample mean
ESS — Explained\(\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n(\hat y_i-\bar y)^2\)Variation in fitted values around the sample mean
RSS — Residual\(\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-\hat y_i)^2\)Variation left unexplained by the fitted model
\[\boxed{\operatorname{TSS}=\operatorname{ESS}+\operatorname{RSS}}\]

This exact decomposition holds for in-sample OLS with an intercept.

Derivation of the sums-of-squares decomposition

Add and subtract the fitted value inside each deviation:

\[\begin{aligned}y_i-\bar y&=(y_i-\hat y_i)+(\hat y_i-\bar y)\\&=e_i+(\hat y_i-\bar y).\end{aligned}\]

Square both sides and sum over all observations:

\[\begin{aligned}\sum_i(y_i-\bar y)^2&=\sum_i[e_i+(\hat y_i-\bar y)]^2\\&=\sum_i e_i^2+\sum_i(\hat y_i-\bar y)^2+2\sum_i e_i(\hat y_i-\bar y)\\&=\operatorname{RSS}+\operatorname{ESS}+2\sum_i e_i(\hat y_i-\bar y).\end{aligned}\]

From the normal equations and residual orthogonality, \(X^T\mathbf e=\mathbf 0\). Since \(\widehat{\mathbf y}=X\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}\), we have \(\widehat{\mathbf y}^{T}\mathbf e=0\). If the model contains an intercept, the column of ones also gives \(\sum_i e_i=0\).

\[\begin{aligned}\sum_i e_i(\hat y_i-\bar y)&=\sum_i e_i\hat y_i-\bar y\sum_i e_i\\&=0-\bar y\cdot 0=0.\\\therefore\quad\operatorname{TSS}&=\operatorname{ESS}+\operatorname{RSS}.\end{aligned}\]

Coefficient of Determination — R²

\(R^2\) measures the proportion of observed variation around the sample mean accounted for by the fitted regression.

\[\boxed{R^2=1-\frac{\operatorname{RSS}}{\operatorname{TSS}}=1-\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-\hat y_i)^2}{\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-\bar y)^2}}\]

For in-sample OLS with an intercept and \(\operatorname{TSS}>0\), the decomposition above gives

\[R^2=\frac{\operatorname{ESS}}{\operatorname{TSS}},\qquad 0\le R^2\le1.\]

Interpretation: near 1 means most of the observed variation is explained; near 0 means little improvement over predicting \(\bar y\). A low \(R^2\) does not necessarily imply that the coefficients are statistically insignificant.

\(R^2\) is unitless and never decreases when predictors are added to nested, in-sample OLS models fitted on the same data. Even irrelevant predictors can improve training fit, so maximizing \(R^2\) alone encourages overfitting.

When can R² be negative?

Using the definition \(1-\operatorname{RSS}/\operatorname{TSS}\), a negative value occurs when \(\operatorname{RSS}>\operatorname{TSS}\): the predictions are worse, in squared-error terms, than predicting the mean of the evaluated responses. This can happen on test data, with an OLS model fitted without an intercept, or with other constrained or non-OLS fits. It cannot happen for in-sample OLS with an intercept, because predicting the sample mean is itself a feasible fit. If all evaluated responses are constant, the usual formula is undefined.

Simple Regression — R² and Squared Correlation

For in-sample OLS with one predictor and an intercept, when both predictor and response have nonzero sample variance,

\[\boxed{R^2=r_{xy}^2,\qquad r_{xy}=\operatorname{sgn}(\hat\beta_1)\sqrt{R^2}}\]

\(R^2\) does not preserve the sign of the relationship; the slope or Pearson correlation does.

From the least-squares slope to squared correlation

Use the notation and coefficient formulas derived in Simple Linear Regression — Equivalent Forms of the Slope:

\[\begin{aligned}S_{xx}&=\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2,& S_{yy}&=\sum_i(y_i-\bar y)^2,\\S_{xy}&=\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y),&\hat\beta_1&=\frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}}.\end{aligned}\]

The fitted line passes through \((\bar x,\bar y)\), so

\[\begin{aligned}\hat y_i&=\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1x_i\\&=\bar y-\hat\beta_1\bar x+\hat\beta_1 x_i,\\\hat y_i-\bar y&=\hat\beta_1(x_i-\bar x).\end{aligned}\]

Substitute into the explained sum of squares:

\[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ESS}&=\sum_i(\hat y_i-\bar y)^2\\&=\sum_i[\hat\beta_1(x_i-\bar x)]^2\\&=\hat\beta_1^2 S_{xx}\\&=\left(\frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}}\right)^2S_{xx}=\frac{S_{xy}^2}{S_{xx}}.\end{aligned}\]

Divide by \(\operatorname{TSS}=S_{yy}\):

\[\begin{aligned}R^2&=\frac{\operatorname{ESS}}{\operatorname{TSS}}\\&=\frac{S_{xy}^2}{S_{xx}S_{yy}}\\&=\left(\frac{S_{xy}}{\sqrt{S_{xx}S_{yy}}}\right)^2= r_{xy}^2.\end{aligned}\]

For multiple regression, the analogous identity is \(R^2=\operatorname{Corr}(y,\hat y)^2\) on the fitting sample for OLS with an intercept and nonconstant fitted values. In general, it is not the squared correlation between the response and any single predictor.

Multiple Regression — Two Correlated Predictors

For two centered, standardized predictors \(X_1,X_2\) and a centered, standardized response \(Y\), define the sample correlations

\[r_1=\operatorname{Corr}(X_1,Y),\qquad r_2=\operatorname{Corr}(X_2,Y),\qquad \rho=\operatorname{Corr}(X_1,X_2).\]

When \(|\rho|<1\), the joint in-sample OLS regression has

\[\boxed{R_{\mathrm{joint}}^2=\frac{r_1^2+r_2^2-2\rho r_1r_2}{1-\rho^2}}\]

If the predictors are uncorrelated (\(\rho=0\)), the individual simple-regression \(R^2\) values add. Otherwise, their sum is generally incorrect: shared information can reduce the joint value relative to the sum, while complementary or suppressor effects can increase it.

Derivation using the standardized normal equations

Let \(Z\) contain the two standardized predictor columns and \(\mathbf z_y\) be the standardized response. Their sample variances are 1, and all means are zero, so the intercept is zero. Then

\[C=\frac{Z^TZ}{n-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1&\rho\\\rho&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad \mathbf r=\frac{Z^T\mathbf z_y}{n-1}=\begin{pmatrix}r_1\\r_2\end{pmatrix}.\]

From the OLS normal equations,

\[\begin{aligned}\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}&=C^{-1}\mathbf r\\&=\frac{1}{1-\rho^2}\begin{pmatrix}1&-\rho\\-\rho&1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}r_1\\r_2\end{pmatrix}.\end{aligned}\]

Since the centered fitted values are \(Z\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}\) and \(\operatorname{TSS}=n-1\),

\[\begin{aligned}R_{\mathrm{joint}}^2&=\frac{\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}^TZ^TZ\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}}{n-1}\\&=\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}^TC\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}\\&=\mathbf r^TC^{-1}\mathbf r\\&=\frac{r_1^2+r_2^2-2\rho r_1r_2}{1-\rho^2}.\end{aligned}\]

Subtract the first simple-regression value:

\[R_{\mathrm{joint}}^2-r_1^2=\frac{(r_2-\rho r_1)^2}{1-\rho^2}\ge0.\]

The same argument holds for \(r_2^2\). Together with the upper bound for in-sample OLS,

\[\boxed{\max(r_1^2,r_2^2)\le R_{\mathrm{joint}}^2\le1}\]

Adjusted R²

Ordinary \(R^2\) does not penalize additional predictors. Adjusted \(R^2\) compares residual variation per remaining degree of freedom with total variation per degree of freedom. Here \(p\) is the number of predictors, excluding the intercept, and the design matrix has full column rank.

\[\boxed{R_{\mathrm{adj}}^2=1-\frac{\operatorname{RSS}/(n-p-1)}{\operatorname{TSS}/(n-1)}=1-(1-R^2)\frac{n-1}{n-p-1}}\]

Derivation from residual and total variance

For a model with an intercept and \(n>p+1\), the unbiased error variance estimate under the classical assumptions is \(\hat\sigma_\varepsilon^2=\operatorname{RSS}/(n-p-1)\), whose square root is the residual standard error (RSE). The sample variance of the response is \(s_y^2=\operatorname{TSS}/(n-1)\).

\[\begin{aligned}R_{\mathrm{adj}}^2&=1-\frac{\hat\sigma_\varepsilon^2}{s_y^2}\\&=1-\frac{\operatorname{RSS}/(n-p-1)}{\operatorname{TSS}/(n-1)}\\&=1-\frac{\operatorname{RSS}}{\operatorname{TSS}}\frac{n-1}{n-p-1}\\&=1-(1-R^2)\frac{n-1}{n-p-1}.\end{aligned}\]

Adjusted \(R^2\) can decrease when adding a predictor and can be negative. It is useful for comparing models on the same response and fitting sample, but does not directly measure generalization. For a regression without an intercept, the residual degrees of freedom are \(n-p\); an uncentered version of adjusted \(R^2\) uses \(\operatorname{TSS}_0=\sum_i y_i^2\) with \(n\) total degrees of freedom and is not directly comparable to the centered version.

Akaike and Bayesian Information Criteria

Unlike \(R^2\), AIC and BIC use the maximized likelihood and explicitly penalize model complexity. Both should be minimized when comparing models fitted to the same observations and response on a comparable likelihood scale.

CriterionDefinitionInterpretation
AIC — Akaike information criterion\(-2\log\mathcal L^*+2k\)Targets expected predictive information loss; typically favors less aggressive complexity penalization
BIC — Bayesian information criterion\(-2\log\mathcal L^*+k\log n\)More strongly penalizes complexity when \(n>e^2\); under suitable assumptions favors identifying the true model if it is among the candidates

\(\mathcal L^*\) is the maximized likelihood, \(n\) is the sample size, and \(k\) counts all estimated likelihood parameters. For Gaussian linear regression with an intercept, \(k=p+2\): \(p\) slopes, one intercept and one error variance parameter. Without an intercept, \(k=p+1\).

Both criteria balance fit and complexity. BIC tends to select simpler models than AIC for larger samples. Use them as relative model-selection measures; if the primary goal is predictive performance, prefer cross-validation or independent test-set error.

See How to Train — Maximum Likelihood Estimation for the Gaussian likelihood.

AIC for Gaussian linear regression

Consider a regression model with conditional mean \(f(x_i;\boldsymbol\beta)\) and independent Gaussian errors with common variance \(\sigma_\varepsilon^2\):

\[y_i=f(x_i;\boldsymbol\beta)+\varepsilon_i,\qquad \varepsilon_i\mid X\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma_\varepsilon^2).\]

For models fitted to the same observations, the AIC can be computed directly from their residual sums of squares (assuming positive RSS):

\[\boxed{\operatorname{AIC}=n\log\!\left(\frac{\operatorname{RSS}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta})}{n}\right)+2k+C_n},\qquad C_n=n[1+\log(2\pi)].\]

The constant \(C_n\) is common to all these models and may be omitted when comparing them.

Derivation: from Gaussian likelihood to AIC

Using conditional independence, multiply the Gaussian densities:

\[\begin{aligned} \mathcal L(\boldsymbol\beta,\sigma_\varepsilon^2\mid X,y) &=\prod_{i=1}^n\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma_\varepsilon^2}}\exp\!\left[-\frac{(y_i-f(x_i;\boldsymbol\beta))^2}{2\sigma_\varepsilon^2}\right]\\ &=(2\pi\sigma_\varepsilon^2)^{-n/2}\exp\!\left[-\frac{\operatorname{RSS}(\boldsymbol\beta)}{2\sigma_\varepsilon^2}\right]. \end{aligned}\]

Taking the logarithm,

\[\begin{aligned} \ell(\boldsymbol\beta,\sigma_\varepsilon^2) &=-\frac n2\log(2\pi)-\frac n2\log(\sigma_\varepsilon^2)-\frac{\operatorname{RSS}(\boldsymbol\beta)}{2\sigma_\varepsilon^2}. \end{aligned}\]

From the MLE derivation, the estimated variance is \(\widehat{\sigma}_{\varepsilon,\mathrm{MLE}}^2=\operatorname{RSS}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta})/n\). Substituting both maximum likelihood estimates gives

\[\begin{aligned} \ell_{\max}&=-\frac n2\log(2\pi)-\frac n2\log\!\left(\frac{\operatorname{RSS}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta})}{n}\right) -\frac{\operatorname{RSS}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta})}{2\,\operatorname{RSS}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta})/n}\\ &=-\frac n2\left[\log(2\pi)+\log\!\left(\frac{\operatorname{RSS}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta})}{n}\right)+1\right]. \end{aligned}\]

Therefore,

\[\begin{aligned} \operatorname{AIC}&=-2\ell_{\max}+2k\\ &=n\log(2\pi)+n\log\!\left(\frac{\operatorname{RSS}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta})}{n}\right)+n+2k. \end{aligned}\]

Dropping the common constant leaves \(n\log(\operatorname{RSS}/n)+2k\) for relative comparisons.

How to calculate the maximized likelihood

  1. Fit each candidate model to the same dataset to obtain its coefficient MLEs (OLS for Gaussian linear regression).
  2. Calculate the fitted residuals \(e_i=y_i-\hat y_i\) and \(\operatorname{RSS}=\sum_{i=1}^n e_i^2\).
  3. Estimate the error variance using \(\widehat{\sigma}_{\varepsilon,\mathrm{MLE}}^2=\operatorname{RSS}/n\).
  4. Substitute the estimates into the log-likelihood to obtain \(\ell_{\max}\), then compute \(\operatorname{AIC}=-2\ell_{\max}+2k\).

Although the unbiased classical error variance estimator with an intercept is \(\operatorname{RSS}/(n-p-1)\), use the MLE \(\operatorname{RSS}/n\) for AIC because the likelihood must be maximized. Count the variance as an estimated parameter unless it is known.

Relative likelihood of candidate models

Let \(\operatorname{AIC}_{\min}\) denote the smallest AIC among the candidate models. Define the AIC difference and relative likelihood of model \(M_i\) as

\[\Delta_i=\operatorname{AIC}_i-\operatorname{AIC}_{\min},\qquad \boxed{\mathcal R_i=\exp(-\Delta_i/2)}.\]

The best-scoring model has relative likelihood 1. Smaller values indicate weaker relative support according to AIC, not the probability that a model is true.

Example: compare linear, quadratic and cubic models

Fit the following three models on the same dataset, estimating the intercept, slope coefficients and common Gaussian error variance for each model.

ModelRegression meanParameters \(k\)\(\ell_{\max}\)AIC
Linear\(\beta_0+\beta_1x\)3\(-210\)\(2(3)-2(-210)=426\)
Quadratic\(\beta_0+\beta_1x+\beta_2x^2\)4\(-202\)\(2(4)-2(-202)=412\)
Cubic\(\beta_0+\beta_1x+\beta_2x^2+\beta_3x^3\)5\(-201\)\(2(5)-2(-201)=412\)

The quadratic and cubic models tie for the lowest AIC, \(\operatorname{AIC}_{\min}=412\). The relative likelihoods are

\[\begin{aligned} \mathcal R_{\mathrm{linear}}&=\exp\!\left(\frac{412-426}{2}\right)=e^{-7}\approx0.000912,\\ \mathcal R_{\mathrm{quadratic}}&=\exp\!\left(\frac{412-412}{2}\right)=1,\\ \mathcal R_{\mathrm{cubic}}&=\exp\!\left(\frac{412-412}{2}\right)=1. \end{aligned}\]

AIC provides equal support for the quadratic and cubic models, and much less support for the linear model. The quadratic model is a reasonable choice if simplicity is preferred: the cubic model's improvement of one log-likelihood unit exactly offsets its additional parameter penalty.

Diagnostics

Visual Inspection of Residuals

Diagnostics assess whether the fitted model is appropriate and whether statistical inference is reliable. Always inspect the residuals in addition to running formal tests. Systematic patterns may reveal missing structure that a good in-sample \(R^2\) alone cannot detect.

\[e_i=y_i-\hat y_i.\]
Diagnostic plotWhat to look forPotential remedies
Residuals vs fitted values / each predictorRandom scatter around zero is desirable. Curvature or clusters suggest misspecified mean structure.Add nonlinear terms, interactions or relevant predictors.
Residuals vs fitted values / scale-location plotFanning or changing spread suggests heteroskedasticity. Scale-location plots use \(\sqrt{|r_i|}\) for standardized residuals \(r_i\).Transform the response where appropriate, use WLS or robust standard errors.
Residuals vs time or observation order; residual ACFRuns, trends, periodicity or significant autocorrelation suggest dependent errors.Model temporal structure; use GLS, HAC or cluster-robust standard errors as appropriate.
Residuals vs predictors or groupsSystematic patterns, group differences or missing interactions. A zero sample linear correlation with included predictors is automatic in OLS.Improve the specification; investigate omitted confounders separately.

Outliers, Leverage and Influence

An outlier is unusual in its response relative to the fitted model, high leverage means an unusual predictor configuration, and influence measures how much the fitted model changes if an observation is removed.

MeasureDefinition and screening ruleInterpretation
Leverage\(h_{ii}=H_{ii}\), where \(H=X(X^TX)^{-1}X^T\). Average leverage is \((p+1)/n\) with intercept; flag \(h_{ii}>2(p+1)/n\).Unusual predictor values or combinations. High leverage can pull the fit toward the observation.
Studentized residual\(r_i=e_i/[s\sqrt{1-h_{ii}}]\). Externally studentized residuals use the error scale estimated without observation \(i\). Flag \(|r_i|>2\) for review; \(>3\) is a stronger warning.Unusually large response error relative to its estimated variability.

Here \(p\) is the number of predictors excluding the intercept, \(s^2=\mathrm{RSS}/(n-p-1)\), and the model has full column rank. See the projection matrix for the definition of \(H\).

How to validate: inspect studentized residuals vs leverage and refit with and without flagged points to compare coefficients, intervals and predictions.

Potential remedies: investigate data-entry errors, unusual populations or missing structure; consider robust regression where justified. Do not automatically remove valid observations solely because a heuristic flags them.

Normality of Error Terms

Normality of the conditional errors is an additional assumption for the usual exact finite-sample Gaussian \(t\)- and \(F\)-inference. It is not required for OLS unbiasedness or BLUE. Residuals approximate the unobserved errors, but are not independent even when the errors are.

CheckHow to interpret
Normal Q–Q plotApproximately straight line: compatible with normality. Curvature: skewness; systematic tail deviations: heavy or light tails.
Histogram of residualsInspect symmetry, tail behavior and multiple modes. Small samples can obscure shape.
Jarque–Bera / Omnibus testNull: normality (as assessed through skewness and kurtosis). Small p-value suggests departure. A large p-value does not establish normality.
Shapiro–WilkAdditional normality screen, especially for smaller samples; interpret residual-based tests with care because fitted residuals are dependent.

Potential remedies: inspect influential points and misspecification first; consider a justified response transformation, robust or bootstrap inference with an appropriate resampling design, or a model with a more suitable response distribution. Large samples may allow asymptotic inference under suitable conditions.

Diagnostic Tests and Multicollinearity

Use the tests below alongside residual plots and knowledge of the data-generating process. A small p-value is evidence against the corresponding null, not a measure of the severity of the problem.

ProblemDiagnosticNull / interpretation
Nonlinearity / misspecificationRamsey RESETNull: added powers of fitted values do not improve the specified model in the tested direction. A rejection flags possible misspecification, not its cause.
HeteroskedasticityBreusch–Pagan / WhiteNull: constant conditional error variance (against the alternatives tested).
Serial correlationDurbin–Watson / Breusch–GodfreyDW near 2 suggests little first-order autocorrelation; near 0 positive and near 4 negative. BG tests no serial correlation through a specified lag order.
MulticollinearityVIF, correlation matrix, rank and condition numberHigh VIF indicates a predictor can be explained by other predictors. Rank deficiency indicates perfect collinearity. A large condition number can also reflect scaling.

Variance inflation factor (VIF)

\[\mathrm{VIF}_j=\frac{1}{1-R_j^2}.\]

Regress predictor \(j\) on all other predictors (with an intercept) to obtain \(R_j^2\). A VIF above 5 is a common warning heuristic, not a universal threshold. If \(R_j^2=1\), the predictor is perfectly collinear. See No Perfect Multicollinearity.

Potential remedies: evaluate correlations and redundancy, select representative predictors, or consider PCA or regularization. Standardize predictors before interpreting a scale-sensitive condition number. VIF can identify joint collinearity that pairwise correlations miss.

Interpreting the OLS Diagnostic Output

The diagnostic statistics at the bottom of the statsmodels.api.OLS summary help identify departures from the model assumptions.

Example: regression of five-day returns

StatisticOLS outputInterpretation and consequences
Omnibus33104.830Joint test of normality based on skewness and kurtosis. A large statistic indicates a departure from normality.
Prob(Omnibus)0.000Very small p-value: reject normality using the usual test reference distribution. Exact Gaussian small-sample inference may be unreliable.
Skew−0.780Normality benchmark: 0. Negative skewness indicates asymmetry toward negative residuals, suggesting a greater risk of large negative errors.
Kurtosis19.205Normality benchmark: 3 (Pearson kurtosis). This very high value indicates unusually large tail contributions; Gaussian error intervals may underestimate extreme-error risk.
Durbin–Watson0.436Far below 2: strong evidence of positive first-order residual autocorrelation. Conventional OLS standard errors may be underestimated.
Jarque–Bera (JB)1211101.670Normality test based on departures of skewness from 0 and kurtosis from 3. The large statistic flags substantial nonnormality.
Prob(JB)0.00Very small p-value under the usual reference distribution: evidence against normality. Check the residual distribution and use suitable inference methods.
Cond. No.79.8Measures numerical conditioning of the design matrix. Check predictor scaling and VIF before attributing this value to multicollinearity; poor conditioning can make coefficients unstable.

Displayed p-values of zero are rounded, not literally zero. Because the residuals are serially correlated here, interpret conventional normality-test p-values with caution.

Practical interpretation

Residual distribution: negative skewness and high kurtosis suggest asymmetric errors and extreme deviations from the Gaussian model. Inspect the histogram against a fitted normal density and the Q–Q plot.

Residual autocorrelation: the supplied example shows positive residual autocorrelation through lag 4. Consecutive five-day returns share four daily returns, so overlapping targets can generate serial dependence. Inspect the residual ACF; consider HAC standard errors with a suitable lag bandwidth for inference, or non-overlapping targets where appropriate.

Inference

Inference and the Error Assumptions

Heteroskedasticity occurs when error variance differs across observations. Larger error variance for predictor values far from their mean can lead to underestimated OLS standard errors, inflated t-statistics in absolute value and false discoveries. See Model Assumptions — Homoskedasticity (5a) for diagnostics and remedies: robust standard errors, response transformations and weighted least squares.

Serial correlation occurs when errors from consecutive observations are correlated, violating assumption 5b. Positive serial correlation can lead to underestimated OLS standard errors, inflated t-statistics in absolute value and false discoveries. See Model Assumptions — No correlation between error terms (5b) for remedies: HAC standard errors and models that account for error dependence.

The Durbin–Watson statistic diagnoses first-order serial correlation in OLS residuals. The usual test considers no first-order error autocorrelation against an autoregressive alternative.

\[DW=\frac{\sum_{i=2}^{n}(e_i-e_{i-1})^2}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}e_i^2}\approx 2(1-\hat\rho_1).\]

It ranges from 0 to 4: values near 2 suggest no first-order autocorrelation, lower values suggest positive autocorrelation, and higher values suggest negative autocorrelation. Formal critical bounds depend on the number of predictors, observations and significance level and are obtained from Durbin–Watson tables under the test's conditions. A value near 2 does not rule out other forms of dependence.

Classical inference

Inference aims to draw conclusions from sample data about relationships in the population, including the significance of individual coefficients, the overall regression and confidence intervals. In addition to the Gauss–Markov assumptions, exact classical finite-sample inference assumes normally distributed errors conditional on the predictors:

\[\boldsymbol\varepsilon\mid X\sim\mathcal N_n(\mathbf0,\sigma_\varepsilon^2 I_n),\qquad \mathbf y\mid X\sim\mathcal N_n(X\boldsymbol\beta,\sigma_\varepsilon^2 I_n).\]

This assumption often fails in practice, but the test statistics used under normality are also approximately valid in large samples with appropriate standard errors.

Throughout, \(p\) denotes the number of predictors excluding the intercept. Unless stated otherwise, the model includes an intercept and has \(n-p-1\) residual degrees of freedom.

Simple Linear Regression — Accuracy of Coefficient Estimates

Consider \(y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i+\varepsilon_i\). How much do the coefficient estimates vary across repeated samples with the same predictor values? Under exogeneity, the OLS estimates are unbiased. Using the previously derived OLS estimators, define

\[S_{xx}=\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)^2,\qquad \hat\beta_1=\frac{\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y)}{S_{xx}},\qquad \hat\beta_0=\bar y-\hat\beta_1\bar x.\]

Under assumptions 1–5, conditional on \(X\),

\[\boxed{\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta_1\mid X)=\frac{\sigma_\varepsilon^2}{S_{xx}}},\qquad \boxed{\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta_0\mid X)=\sigma_\varepsilon^2\left(\frac1n+\frac{\bar x^2}{S_{xx}}\right)}.\]

Variance of the slope

Since \(\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)=0\), the slope is a weighted sum of the responses:

\[\begin{aligned}\hat\beta_1&=\frac{\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)y_i-\bar y\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)}{S_{xx}}\\&=\sum_i w_i y_i,\qquad w_i=\frac{x_i-\bar x}{S_{xx}},\qquad \sum_iw_i=0.\end{aligned}\]

Conditional on the predictors, \(\operatorname{Var}(y_i\mid X)=\sigma_\varepsilon^2\) and distinct responses are uncorrelated under assumption 5.

\[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta_1\mid X)&=\operatorname{Var}\left(\sum_iw_iy_i\mid X\right)\\&=\sum_i w_i^2\operatorname{Var}(y_i\mid X)\\&=\sigma_\varepsilon^2\sum_i\frac{(x_i-\bar x)^2}{S_{xx}^2}\\&=\frac{\sigma_\varepsilon^2}{S_{xx}^2}S_{xx}=\frac{\sigma_\varepsilon^2}{S_{xx}}.\end{aligned}\]

Variance of the intercept

\[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{Var}(\bar y\mid X)&=\frac{1}{n^2}\sum_i\operatorname{Var}(y_i\mid X)=\frac{\sigma_\varepsilon^2}{n},\\\operatorname{Cov}(\bar y,\hat\beta_1\mid X)&=\operatorname{Cov}\left(\frac1n\sum_i y_i,\sum_j w_j y_j\mid X\right)\\&=\frac1n\sum_i\sum_j w_j\operatorname{Cov}(y_i,y_j\mid X)\\&=\frac{\sigma_\varepsilon^2}{n}\sum_iw_i=0.\end{aligned}\]

Substituting these results into the variance of the intercept:

\[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta_0\mid X)&=\operatorname{Var}(\bar y-\bar x\hat\beta_1\mid X)\\&=\operatorname{Var}(\bar y\mid X)+\bar x^2\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta_1\mid X)\\&\quad-2\bar x\operatorname{Cov}(\bar y,\hat\beta_1\mid X)\\&=\sigma_\varepsilon^2\left(\frac1n+\frac{\bar x^2}{S_{xx}}\right).\end{aligned}\]

Covariance between intercept and slope

\[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{Cov}(\hat\beta_0,\hat\beta_1\mid X)&=\operatorname{Cov}(\bar y-\bar x\hat\beta_1,\hat\beta_1\mid X)\\&=\operatorname{Cov}(\bar y,\hat\beta_1\mid X)-\bar x\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta_1\mid X)\\&=-\frac{\bar x\sigma_\varepsilon^2}{S_{xx}}.\end{aligned}\]

Because the true error variance is unknown, use its unbiased estimate (two fitted coefficients, so \(p=1\)):

\[s^2=\widehat\sigma_\varepsilon^2=\frac{\operatorname{RSS}}{n-2}=\frac{1}{n-2}\sum_i(y_i-\hat y_i)^2.\]

Estimated standard errors

\[\boxed{\operatorname{SE}(\hat\beta_1)=\frac{s}{\sqrt{S_{xx}}}},\qquad \boxed{\operatorname{SE}(\hat\beta_0)=s\sqrt{\frac1n+\frac{\bar x^2}{S_{xx}}}}.\]

The more spread out the predictor values, the more precise the slope estimate, all else equal. Centering the predictor makes the intercept and slope estimators uncorrelated and the intercept corresponds to the expected response at the original predictor mean.

Simple Linear Regression — Confidence Intervals and Hypothesis Tests

To test whether the predictor is linearly associated with the response, test \(H_0:\beta_1=0\) against \(H_1:\beta_1\ne0\). More generally, for either coefficient \(j=0,1\), test \(H_0:\beta_j=\beta_j^{(0)}\).

\[t_j=\frac{\hat\beta_j-\beta_j^{(0)}}{\operatorname{SE}(\hat\beta_j)}\overset{H_0}{\sim}t_{n-2}.\]

The residual degrees of freedom are \(n-2\) because two coefficients are estimated: one for the predictor (slope) and one for the intercept.

The statistic measures how many estimated standard errors the coefficient is from its hypothesized value. Under the classical Gaussian assumptions the two-sided p-value is

\[p\text{-value}=2\Pr(T_{n-2}\ge |t_j|).\]

Reject \(H_0\) if the p-value is below the chosen significance level \(\alpha\). A small p-value is evidence against the null, not the probability that the null is true. Failure to reject does not prove that the coefficient is zero.

Confidence intervals

\[\boxed{\hat\beta_j\pm t_{n-2,\,1-\alpha/2}\operatorname{SE}(\hat\beta_j)}.\]

A 95% confidence interval is constructed by a procedure that contains the true coefficient in 95% of repeated samples under the model assumptions. If it excludes zero, the corresponding two-sided test rejects at the 5% level.

Confidence levelLarge-sample normal critical value
90%1.645
95%1.960
99%2.576

With many residual degrees of freedom, the t-distribution approaches the standard normal distribution; for small samples use the actual t critical value.

Example: TV advertising and sales

CoefficientEstimateStd. errort-statisticp-value
Intercept7.03250.457815.36<0.0001
TV0.04750.002717.67<0.0001

Both coefficients are statistically different from zero at conventional significance levels. The slope indicates a positive linear association between advertising and sales; the intercept estimates expected sales when TV expenditure is zero. This is an association, not necessarily a causal effect.

Multiple Linear Regression — Distribution and Accuracy of Coefficients

Consider the full-column-rank model \(\mathbf y=X\boldsymbol\beta+\boldsymbol\varepsilon\), with \(X\in\mathbb R^{n\times(p+1)}\) and \(\boldsymbol\beta\in\mathbb R^{p+1}\). The estimator is

\[\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}=(X^TX)^{-1}X^T\mathbf y=\boldsymbol\beta+(X^TX)^{-1}X^T\boldsymbol\varepsilon.\]

From the derivations in Model Assumptions — Exogeneity and Homoskedasticity and Uncorrelated Errors,

\[\mathbb E[\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}\mid X]=\boldsymbol\beta,\qquad \operatorname{Cov}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}\mid X)=\sigma_\varepsilon^2(X^TX)^{-1}.\]

Adding Gaussian errors, the estimator is an affine transformation of a multivariate normal vector, so

\[\boxed{\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}\mid X\sim\mathcal N_{p+1}\left(\boldsymbol\beta,\sigma_\varepsilon^2(X^TX)^{-1}\right)}.\]

Hat matrix and residuals

Using the projection matrix and residual orthogonality derived earlier, denote the hat matrix by \(H=P_X\) and the residual-maker matrix by \(M\):

\[H=X(X^TX)^{-1}X^T,\qquad M=I_n-H,\qquad \hat{\mathbf y}=H\mathbf y,\qquad \mathbf e=M\mathbf y.\]

Projection identities

\[\begin{aligned}HX&=X(X^TX)^{-1}X^TX=X,\\MX&=X-HX=0,\\\mathbf e&=M(X\boldsymbol\beta+\boldsymbol\varepsilon)=M\boldsymbol\varepsilon,\\X^T\mathbf e&=\mathbf0,\\\mathbf e^T\hat{\mathbf y}&=\mathbf e^TX\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}=0.\end{aligned}\]

Each fitted value is a weighted sum of the observed responses, \(\hat y_i=\sum_{j=1}^n h_{ij}y_j\). The diagonal \(h_{ii}\) measures leverage (see Diagnostics — Outliers, Leverage and Influence).

Unbiased estimator of the error variance

\[\boxed{s^2=\widehat\sigma_\varepsilon^2=\frac{\operatorname{RSS}}{n-p-1}},\qquad \mathbb E[s^2\mid X]=\sigma_\varepsilon^2.\]

Why the denominator is \(n-p-1\)

Since \(M\) is symmetric and idempotent, and \(\operatorname{rank}(H)=p+1\),

\[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{RSS}&=\mathbf e^T\mathbf e=\boldsymbol\varepsilon^TM^TM\boldsymbol\varepsilon=\boldsymbol\varepsilon^TM\boldsymbol\varepsilon,\\\mathbb E[\operatorname{RSS}\mid X]&=\operatorname{tr}\left(M\mathbb E[\boldsymbol\varepsilon\boldsymbol\varepsilon^T\mid X]\right)\\&=\sigma_\varepsilon^2\operatorname{tr}(M)\\&=\sigma_\varepsilon^2\big(n-\operatorname{tr}(H)\big)\\&=\sigma_\varepsilon^2(n-p-1).\end{aligned}\]

Dividing by the residual degrees of freedom gives an unbiased estimator of the variance (not necessarily of the standard deviation).

Under Gaussian errors, the orthogonal projection \(M\) has rank \(n-p-1\); thus the residual sum of squares is a scaled chi-square random variable:

\[\boxed{\frac{(n-p-1)s^2}{\sigma_\varepsilon^2}=\frac{\operatorname{RSS}}{\sigma_\varepsilon^2}\mid X\sim\chi^2_{n-p-1}}.\]

Moreover, \(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}\) and \(s^2\) are independent conditional on \(X\), since they are functions of orthogonal Gaussian projections. Without an intercept, use \(n-p\) residual degrees of freedom instead.

Multiple Linear Regression — Individual Coefficient Tests

Question: is the j-th coefficient equal to a hypothesized value (typically zero), holding the other predictors fixed?

\[H_0:\beta_j=\beta_j^{(0)},\qquad H_1:\beta_j\ne\beta_j^{(0)}.\]

Let \(v_j=[(X^TX)^{-1}]_{jj}\), the diagonal element corresponding to coefficient \(j\). From the multivariate distribution,

\[\hat\beta_j\mid X\sim\mathcal N(\beta_j,\sigma_\varepsilon^2v_j),\qquad \operatorname{SE}(\hat\beta_j)=s\sqrt{v_j}.\]

From the normal statistic to the t-statistic

Under the null, with known error variance, the standardized coefficient follows a standard normal distribution. Let \(\nu=n-p-1\). With unknown variance, use the independent chi-square variance estimator from above:

\[Z=\frac{\hat\beta_j-\beta_j^{(0)}}{\sigma_\varepsilon\sqrt{v_j}}\sim\mathcal N(0,1),\qquad U=\frac{\nu s^2}{\sigma_\varepsilon^2}\sim\chi^2_\nu.\]
\[\begin{aligned}T&=\frac{Z}{\sqrt{U/\nu}}\\&=\frac{(\hat\beta_j-\beta_j^{(0)})/(\sigma_\varepsilon\sqrt{v_j})}{s/\sigma_\varepsilon}\\&=\frac{\hat\beta_j-\beta_j^{(0)}}{s\sqrt{v_j}}\sim t_\nu.\end{aligned}\]
\[\boxed{t_j=\frac{\hat\beta_j-\beta_j^{(0)}}{\operatorname{SE}(\hat\beta_j)}},\qquad \boxed{\mathrm{CI}_{1-\alpha}:\ \hat\beta_j\pm t_{n-p-1,\,1-\alpha/2}\operatorname{SE}(\hat\beta_j)}.\]

The interpretation of the p-value and confidence interval is the same as in simple regression, with the updated degrees of freedom.

Multiple testing

Testing many individual coefficients at level \(\alpha\) increases the chance of at least one false positive. For 20 independent tests of true null hypotheses at \(\alpha=0.05\),

\[\Pr(\text{at least one false positive})=1-(1-0.05)^{20}\approx0.642.\]

Regression coefficient tests need not be independent, so the exact probability can differ. For simultaneous individual claims consider multiple-testing adjustments; for a single prespecified group of coefficients, use the joint F-test below.

Multiple Linear Regression — Overall and Partial F-tests

Overall significance: are all slope coefficients zero?

\[H_0:\beta_1=\cdots=\beta_p=0,\qquad H_1:\text{at least one slope is nonzero}.\]

Compare the full regression with the intercept-only model. The latter predicts \(\bar y\), so its residual sum of squares is TSS. Using the sums-of-squares decomposition,

\[\boxed{F=\frac{(\operatorname{TSS}-\operatorname{RSS})/p}{\operatorname{RSS}/(n-p-1)}=\frac{\operatorname{ESS}/p}{\operatorname{RSS}/(n-p-1)}}\overset{H_0}{\sim}F_{p,n-p-1}.\]

Under \(H_0\), both the numerator and denominator have conditional expectation \(\sigma_\varepsilon^2\), giving the intuition that F is typically of order 1 (its exact mean is not generally 1). Under the alternative the numerator has a larger expectation. A sufficiently large F provides evidence that at least one predictor is associated with the response.

Use the upper-tail p-value \(\Pr(F_{p,n-p-1}\ge F_{\rm obs})\), or compare to the critical value for the appropriate degrees of freedom and significance level. The threshold is not universally 1.

Partial F-test: is a subset of coefficients zero?

Fit two nested models on the same observations and response, both with an intercept. The reduced model has \(p_0\) predictors; the full model has \(p_1\) predictors, with \(p_1>p_0\).

ModelPredictorsResidual sum of squaresResidual degrees of freedom
Reduced (restricted)\(p_0\)\(\operatorname{RSS}_0\)\(n-p_0-1\)
Full (unrestricted)\(p_1\)\(\operatorname{RSS}_1\)\(n-p_1-1\)

The null sets all \(q=p_1-p_0\) additional coefficients to zero; the alternative says at least one is nonzero.

\[\boxed{F=\frac{(\operatorname{RSS}_0-\operatorname{RSS}_1)/(p_1-p_0)}{\operatorname{RSS}_1/(n-p_1-1)}}\overset{H_0}{\sim}F_{p_1-p_0,n-p_1-1}.\]

Why the F distribution arises

Let \(H_0^*,H_1^*\) be the hat matrices of the reduced and full models, respectively. Because their column spaces are nested, \(D=H_1^*-H_0^*\) is an orthogonal projector of rank \(q\), orthogonal to the full model residual projector \(M_1=I_n-H_1^*\). Under the null, the true mean belongs to the reduced column space.

\[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{RSS}_0-\operatorname{RSS}_1&=\mathbf y^TD\mathbf y=\boldsymbol\varepsilon^TD\boldsymbol\varepsilon,\\\operatorname{RSS}_1&=\boldsymbol\varepsilon^TM_1\boldsymbol\varepsilon.\end{aligned}\]

The two quadratic forms are independent under Gaussian errors because their projections are orthogonal:

\[U=\frac{\operatorname{RSS}_0-\operatorname{RSS}_1}{\sigma_\varepsilon^2}\sim\chi^2_q,\qquad V=\frac{\operatorname{RSS}_1}{\sigma_\varepsilon^2}\sim\chi^2_{n-p_1-1}.\]
\[F=\frac{U/q}{V/(n-p_1-1)}\sim F_{q,n-p_1-1}.\]

The F-test evaluates the reduction in RSS per additional parameter relative to the estimated error variance. It is one joint test, rather than a collection of individual t-tests. It does not identify which coefficients are significant or eliminate multiplicity if many groups are tested. For a single restriction, the classical F-statistic equals the squared t-statistic.

Predictions

Point Estimate

For a given predictor value \(x_0\), the fitted regression equation gives the same point estimate for the mean response \(\mathbb E[Y\mid x_0]\) and an individual new response \(Y_0\):

\[\hat y_0=\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1x_0.\]

Example

Given the fitted line \(\hat y=60+5x\), the point estimate at \(x_0=10\) is \(\hat y_0=60+5(10)=110\).

A point estimate does not quantify uncertainty. A confidence interval estimates the mean response, whereas a prediction interval estimates the range of an individual future observation.

Simple Linear Regression — Confidence and Prediction Intervals

Under the classical assumptions with Gaussian errors, let \(x_0\) be fixed and the new error independent of the training errors. Define

\[S_{xx}=\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)^2,\qquad s^2=\frac{\operatorname{RSS}}{n-2},\qquad h_0=\frac1n+\frac{(x_0-\bar x)^2}{S_{xx}}.\]
IntervalFormula at confidence level \(1-\alpha\)Interpretation
Confidence interval\(\displaystyle\hat y_0\pm t_{1-\alpha/2,n-2}\,s\sqrt{h_0}\)Uncertainty in the estimated conditional mean
Prediction interval\(\displaystyle\hat y_0\pm t_{1-\alpha/2,n-2}\,s\sqrt{1+h_0}\)Uncertainty in an individual new observation

There are \(n-2\) residual degrees of freedom because the intercept and slope are estimated.

Variance of the estimated mean response

Using the previously derived coefficient variances and covariance, with conditioning on the fixed predictors implicit:

\[\begin{aligned} \operatorname{Var}(\hat y_0)&=\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta_0+x_0\hat\beta_1)\\ &=\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta_0)+x_0^2\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta_1)+2x_0\operatorname{Cov}(\hat\beta_0,\hat\beta_1)\\ &=\sigma_\varepsilon^2\left(\frac1n+\frac{\bar x^2}{S_{xx}}\right)+\frac{x_0^2\sigma_\varepsilon^2}{S_{xx}}-\frac{2x_0\bar x\sigma_\varepsilon^2}{S_{xx}}\\ &=\sigma_\varepsilon^2\left(\frac1n+\frac{(x_0-\bar x)^2}{S_{xx}}\right)=\sigma_\varepsilon^2h_0. \end{aligned}\]

Variance of the individual prediction error

A new response is \(Y_0=\beta_0+\beta_1x_0+\varepsilon_0\). Its error is independent of the fitted coefficients, so

\[\begin{aligned} \operatorname{Var}(Y_0-\hat y_0)&=\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_0-\hat y_0)\\ &=\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_0)+\operatorname{Var}(\hat y_0)-2\operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon_0,\hat y_0)\\ &=\sigma_\varepsilon^2+\sigma_\varepsilon^2h_0-0\\ &=\sigma_\varepsilon^2\left(1+\frac1n+\frac{(x_0-\bar x)^2}{S_{xx}}\right). \end{aligned}\]

Replace the unknown \(\sigma_\varepsilon^2\) with \(s^2\) and use the corresponding t critical value to obtain the intervals above.

Both intervals are narrowest at \(x_0=\bar x\) and widen farther from the predictor mean. Increasing the sample size and predictor spread reduces estimation uncertainty. The prediction interval combines the uncertainty of the confidence interval with the additional irreducible uncertainty from the error term, added in quadrature by construction of the model \(Y_0=\beta_0+\beta_1x_0+\varepsilon_0\). The variances add because the new error is independent of the fitted mean:

\[\operatorname{Var}(Y_0-\hat y_0\mid X)=\operatorname{Var}(\hat y_0\mid X)+\sigma_\varepsilon^2.\]

Multiple Linear Regression
