The same reasoning extends to multiple predictors. For a new predictor vector \(\mathbf x_0=(1,x_{01},\ldots,x_{0p})^T\), including the intercept, the point estimate and uncertainty factor are

\[\hat y_0=\mathbf x_0^T\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta},\qquad h_0=\mathbf x_0^T(X^TX)^{-1}\mathbf x_0,\qquad s^2=\frac{\operatorname{RSS}}{n-p-1}.\]

Extension to multiple predictors

Using the coefficient covariance matrix:

\[\begin{aligned} \operatorname{Var}(\hat y_0\mid X)&=\mathbf x_0^T\operatorname{Cov}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}\mid X)\mathbf x_0\\ &=\sigma_\varepsilon^2\mathbf x_0^T(X^TX)^{-1}\mathbf x_0=\sigma_\varepsilon^2h_0,\\ \operatorname{Var}(Y_0-\hat y_0\mid X)&=\sigma_\varepsilon^2(1+h_0). \end{aligned}\]
IntervalFormula
Confidence interval\(\displaystyle\hat y_0\pm t_{1-\alpha/2,n-p-1}\,s\sqrt{h_0}\)
Prediction interval\(\displaystyle\hat y_0\pm t_{1-\alpha/2,n-p-1}\,s\sqrt{1+h_0}\)

Here \(p\) excludes the intercept. These are pointwise intervals under the classical Gaussian model, not simultaneous bands or guarantees for extrapolation.

Regularization

Why Regularize?

With many predictors, the risk of prediction errors due to high variance increases because a complex model is more prone to overfitting. Regularization deliberately introduces bias into the coefficient estimates to reduce variance and potentially lower generalization error. This can improve prediction accuracy and, when irrelevant predictors are removed, model interpretability.

Under the Gauss–Markov assumptions, OLS is BLUE, but it need not minimize out-of-sample prediction error. Regularization adds a penalty to the fitting objective:

\[\text{Regularized loss}=\operatorname{RSS}(\boldsymbol\beta)+\text{penalty}(\boldsymbol\beta).\]

For the derivations below, center the predictors and response so that \(X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}\) contains only predictor columns and \(\boldsymbol\beta\in\mathbb R^p\) contains only slopes. The intercept is not penalized and is recovered as \(\hat\beta_0=\bar y-\sum_{j=1}^p\hat\beta_j\bar x_j\) in the original units.

Constrained Optimization and Lagrange Multipliers

Instead of minimizing RSS freely, restrict the size of the regression coefficients. The two standard constraints are:

MethodConstraintGeometry (two predictors)
Lasso (L1)\(\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^p|\beta_j|\le c\)Diamond
Ridge (L2)\(\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^p\beta_j^2\le c\)Circle of radius \(\sqrt c\)

From constrained to penalized minimization

Write either constraint as \(g(\boldsymbol\beta)\le c\). The optimization problem and its Lagrangian are

\[\begin{aligned}\min_{\boldsymbol\beta}\quad &\operatorname{RSS}(\boldsymbol\beta)\\\text{subject to}\quad &g(\boldsymbol\beta)\le c,\\ \mathcal L(\boldsymbol\beta,\lambda)&=\operatorname{RSS}(\boldsymbol\beta)+\lambda\bigl(g(\boldsymbol\beta)-c\bigr),\qquad\lambda\ge0.\end{aligned}\]

At an optimum, complementary slackness gives \(\lambda(g(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta})-c)=0\). If the restriction is active, the solution lies on the constraint boundary. For a fixed multiplier, \(-\lambda c\) is constant with respect to the coefficients and can be dropped:

\[\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_\lambda=\arg\min_{\boldsymbol\beta}\left\{\operatorname{RSS}(\boldsymbol\beta)+\lambda g(\boldsymbol\beta)\right\}.\]

For L1, the same convex optimization conditions use a subgradient at zero, where the absolute value is not differentiable. For a given penalized solution, choosing \(c=g(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_\lambda)\) recovers a corresponding constrained optimum.

The sharp corners of the L1 constraint favor exact zero coefficients, producing feature selection. The smooth L2 constraint generally shrinks coefficients without eliminating them.

MethodPenalized lossTypical effect
Ridge / L2\(\displaystyle\|\mathbf y-X\boldsymbol\beta\|_2^2+\lambda\sum_{j=1}^p\beta_j^2\)Shrinkage and stability with correlated predictors
Lasso / L1\(\displaystyle\|\mathbf y-X\boldsymbol\beta\|_2^2+\lambda\sum_{j=1}^p|\beta_j|\)Shrinkage and sparse coefficients
Elastic Net\(\displaystyle\|\mathbf y-X\boldsymbol\beta\|_2^2+\lambda_1\|\boldsymbol\beta\|_1+\lambda_2\|\boldsymbol\beta\|_2^2\)Combines sparsity and stability

Ridge Regression — Derivation and Bias

Ridge minimizes RSS plus a squared L2 penalty on the slopes:

\[L_\lambda(\boldsymbol\beta)=\operatorname{RSS}(\boldsymbol\beta)+\lambda\boldsymbol\beta^T\boldsymbol\beta.\]

Derive the Ridge estimator

Use the RSS gradient derived earlier. Differentiate the additional quadratic penalty:

\[\begin{aligned}\nabla_{\boldsymbol\beta}(\lambda\boldsymbol\beta^T\boldsymbol\beta)&=\nabla_{\boldsymbol\beta}\left(\lambda\sum_{j=1}^p\beta_j^2\right)=2\lambda\boldsymbol\beta,\\ \nabla_{\boldsymbol\beta}L_\lambda&=-2X^T(\mathbf y-X\boldsymbol\beta)+2\lambda\boldsymbol\beta.\end{aligned}\]

Set the gradient to zero:

\[\begin{aligned}-2X^T\mathbf y+2X^TX\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_\lambda+2\lambda\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_\lambda&=0,\\ (X^TX+\lambda I_p)\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_\lambda&=X^T\mathbf y,\\ \hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_\lambda&=(X^TX+\lambda I_p)^{-1}X^T\mathbf y.\end{aligned}\]

The Hessian is \(2(X^TX+\lambda I_p)\), which is positive definite for \(\lambda>0\), even when \(X^TX\) is singular. The minimum is therefore unique.

\[\boxed{\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{\mathrm{Ridge}}=(X^TX+\lambda I_p)^{-1}X^T\mathbf y}\]

Why Ridge is biased

Let \(A=X^TX\). Under exogeneity, \(\mathbb E[\boldsymbol\varepsilon\mid X]=0\):

\[\begin{aligned}\mathbb E[\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_\lambda\mid X]&=(A+\lambda I_p)^{-1}X^T\mathbb E[\mathbf y\mid X]\\ &=(A+\lambda I_p)^{-1}A\boldsymbol\beta\\ &=(A+\lambda I_p)^{-1}(A+\lambda I_p-\lambda I_p)\boldsymbol\beta\\ &=\boldsymbol\beta-\lambda(A+\lambda I_p)^{-1}\boldsymbol\beta.\end{aligned}\]
\[\boxed{\operatorname{Bias}(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_\lambda\mid X)=-\lambda(A+\lambda I_p)^{-1}\boldsymbol\beta.}\]

Under homoskedastic and uncorrelated original errors, the covariance follows from the same linear-transformation rule used for OLS. Centering the response does not change the calculation because the centered predictor columns satisfy \(X^T\mathbf 1=0\):

\[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{Cov}(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_\lambda\mid X)&=(A+\lambda I_p)^{-1}X^T(\sigma_\varepsilon^2 I_n)X(A+\lambda I_p)^{-1}\\ &=\sigma_\varepsilon^2(A+\lambda I_p)^{-1}A(A+\lambda I_p)^{-1}.\end{aligned}\]

How the penalty changes the coefficients

For full-column-rank \(X\), compare Ridge with the unregularized OLS estimator in the eigenbasis of the Gram matrix.

Shrinkage in the eigenvector directions

\[A=Q\,\operatorname{diag}(d_1,\ldots,d_p)Q^T,\qquad d_j>0,\quad Q^TQ=I_p.\]
\[\begin{aligned}\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_\lambda&=(A+\lambda I_p)^{-1}A\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{\mathrm{OLS}}\\ &=Q\,\operatorname{diag}\left(\frac{d_j}{d_j+\lambda}\right)Q^T\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}_{\mathrm{OLS}}.\end{aligned}\]

With \(\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}=Q^T\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\), the shrinkage is componentwise:

\[\hat\theta_{\lambda,j}=\frac{d_j}{d_j+\lambda}\hat\theta_{\mathrm{OLS},j},\qquad \operatorname{Var}(\hat\theta_{\lambda,j}\mid X)=\frac{\sigma_\varepsilon^2d_j}{(d_j+\lambda)^2}.\]

Compare with OLS variance \(\sigma_\varepsilon^2/d_j\). Each eigen-direction variance is multiplied by \((d_j/(d_j+\lambda))^2\).

As \(\lambda\) increases, the slopes shrink toward zero. Small eigenvalues are penalized more strongly, stabilizing directions associated with multicollinearity. Shrinkage is exact in the eigenbasis; individual original-coordinate coefficients need not decrease monotonically when predictors are correlated.

Example: two orthogonal predictor directions

Suppose the Gram matrix has eigenvalues \(d_1=100\), \(d_2=1\), and the corresponding OLS coefficients are both 2. With \(\lambda=10\),

\[\hat\theta_{\lambda,1}=\frac{100}{110}(2)\approx1.82,\qquad \hat\theta_{\lambda,2}=\frac{1}{11}(2)\approx0.18.\]

The poorly determined second direction is shrunk much more strongly.

Lasso Regression — Why Coefficients Can Become Zero

Lasso minimizes \(\operatorname{RSS}(\boldsymbol\beta)+\lambda\sum_j|\beta_j|\). Unlike Ridge, its penalty has a kink at zero. In general it is solved numerically, for example with coordinate descent.

One predictor (or an orthogonal predictor column)

For a centered predictor \(\mathbf x\), write \(a=\mathbf x^T\mathbf x>0\) and \(b=\mathbf x^T\mathbf y\). Expanding the objective yields

\[L_\lambda(\beta)=\mathbf y^T\mathbf y-2b\beta+a\beta^2+\lambda|\beta|.\]

For \(\beta\ne0\), differentiating gives \(2a\beta-2b+\lambda\operatorname{sgn}(\beta)=0\). At zero, the subgradient of the absolute value is the interval \([-1,1]\), so zero is optimal if \(|b|\le\lambda/2\).

\[\hat\beta_{\mathrm{Lasso}}=\begin{cases}(b-\lambda/2)/a,&b>\lambda/2,\\0,&|b|\le\lambda/2,\\(b+\lambda/2)/a,&b<-\lambda/2.\end{cases}\]

This soft-thresholding behavior explains why Lasso can remove predictors entirely, whereas Ridge generally keeps nonzero slopes. Elastic Net combines both penalties and can be useful with groups of correlated predictors.

Choosing the Penalty Strength

Choose \(\lambda\) to minimize estimated generalization error, not training RSS. A small penalty gives a model close to OLS; an excessive penalty may cause underfitting.

  1. Choose a logarithmically spaced grid of candidate \(\lambda\) values, including a weak or zero penalty where appropriate.
  2. Use cross-validation to fit the model at each penalty. Center and standardize predictors separately within each training fold.
  3. Calculate the mean validation error (e.g. MSE) for every candidate.
  4. Select the penalty with the lowest validation error, or use the one-standard-error rule: choose the strongest penalty whose mean validation error is within one standard error of the minimum.
  5. Refit with the chosen penalty on the full training set and evaluate once on untouched test data. Use time-ordered or group-based splits when observations are dependent.

For Elastic Net, tune both the overall penalty and the L1/L2 mixture. For inference, remember that choosing the penalty from the data also adds selection uncertainty.

Inference after Regularization

Classical t-tests and F-tests rely on the OLS sampling distribution and its residual sum-of-squares decomposition. These results do not automatically carry over to penalized estimators.

TestWhy the classical version fails
Individual t-testRidge estimates are generally biased and have a different covariance matrix. Lasso additionally performs variable selection, with possible point masses at zero. Using the usual OLS standard errors and t-distribution is not generally valid.
Joint F-testThe ordinary RSS difference and residual degrees of freedom no longer give the classical F-distribution because the penalized fit is not the ordinary least-squares projection.

For prediction, focus on validation performance. When inference is the objective, consider a prespecified OLS model where appropriate, inference on independent data after selection, or methods specifically developed for penalized regression. Refitting OLS on variables selected using the same data does not by itself restore valid p-values.

Model Selection

Why Select Features?

With many predictors, prediction accuracy may suffer because of high model variance and overfitting, and individual effects become harder to interpret. Removing some predictors (setting their coefficients to zero) may introduce bias but reduce variance and improve generalization and interpretability.

Feature selection produces candidate models of different complexity. For a fixed number of predictors, training RSS can identify the best fit; to choose the number of predictors, use a complexity-adjusted criterion or validation performance rather than training RSS alone.

Subset Selection Methods

MethodHow to implement it in practiceConsiderations
Best-subset selectionFor each subset size \(k=0,\ldots,p\), fit OLS on all \(\binom pk\) subsets and keep the one with the lowest training RSS. Select the final size using adjusted \(R^2\), AIC, BIC or cross-validation.Finds the best training fit at each size, but exhaustive search grows exponentially. Practical only for relatively small \(p\), unless specialized search algorithms are used.
Forward-stepwise selectionStart with the intercept-only model. Fit models adding each remaining predictor individually. Keep the addition that reduces RSS the most and repeat, refitting all selected coefficients at each step.Much cheaper than best-subset selection. QR updates can speed up repeated fits. Can start even when \(p\ge n\), but stop before fitting nonidentifiable models. Earlier choices may be suboptimal.
Backward-stepwise selectionStart with all predictors. Remove the predictor whose exclusion increases RSS the least, refit and repeat. For a single deletion under classical OLS, the smallest absolute t-statistic gives the same choice.Requires an identifiable full model and positive residual degrees of freedom if using t-statistics (with intercept, \(n>p+1\)). Earlier removals cannot be reversed.
Forward-stagewise selectionCenter and scale predictors, start with intercept \(\bar y\) and zero slopes. Find the predictor most correlated in absolute value with the current residual and update only its coefficient by a small step in that direction. Recompute residuals and repeat.Useful for high-dimensional problems; may require many iterations. A predictor may be updated repeatedly, unlike forward-stepwise selection. Choose the stopping point by validation.

Number of candidate models

Best-subset selection evaluates \(\binom pk\) models at each size, including one intercept-only model at \(k=0\) and one full model at \(k=p\). The total number is

\[\sum_{k=0}^p\binom pk=2^p.\]

Forward and backward stepwise selection evaluate at most \(1+p+(p-1)+\cdots+1=1+p(p+1)/2\) models each when the full path is feasible.

Forward-stagewise update

Let \(\mathbf e=\mathbf y-\hat{\mathbf y}\) be the current residual vector, and let \(\mathbf x_j\) denote a centered, equally scaled predictor column. The simple regression slope of the residual on this predictor is

\[a_j=\frac{\mathbf x_j^T\mathbf e}{\mathbf x_j^T\mathbf x_j},\qquad j^*=\arg\max_j|\mathbf x_j^T\mathbf e|.\]

Update only the chosen coefficient, \(\beta_{j^*}\leftarrow\beta_{j^*}+\eta a_{j^*}\), with a small step fraction \(0<\eta\le1\). A full step (\(\eta=1\)) gives the residual-regression update in the notes, a greedy coordinate-fitting variant; classical incremental forward stagewise typically uses very small signed steps. Stop by validation or when no useful improvement remains.

Additional Feature Selection Methods

MethodHow to implement it in practiceConsiderations
Correlation screening / VIFInspect correlations among predictors and with the response. Group highly correlated predictors, choose a representative from each group, and check VIF in the remaining design.Fast initial screening. A low marginal correlation with the response does not rule out a useful joint effect. See No Perfect Multicollinearity.
Lasso / Elastic NetFit penalized regression over a grid of penalty strengths using cross-validation. Keep predictors with nonzero coefficients at the selected penalty.Combines fitting and selection. Elastic Net can be more stable for correlated predictors. See Lasso Regression.
RidgeFit Ridge with a validation-selected penalty to shrink coefficients and stabilize prediction.Generally does not set coefficients exactly to zero; it is shrinkage rather than explicit feature selection. See Ridge Regression.
PCA / Principal component regressionCenter and, where appropriate, standardize predictors; fit PCA on training data; retain a subset of principal components and regress the response on their scores. Choose the number of components using validation.Reduces dimension using linear combinations of predictors, not by selecting original variables. High predictor variance does not necessarily imply high predictive value.

Choosing the Best Model

Model selection depends on which models are being compared and whether the goal is inference or prediction.

Models being comparedPreferred criteriaReason
Nested models
One model is a restricted version of another, e.g. linear versus quadratic regression.		AIC or BIC (minimize); adjusted \(R^2\) (maximize). For a formal test of nested OLS restrictions, use a partial F-test under its assumptions.On the same training data, adding predictors to OLS cannot increase RSS or MSE, or decrease \(R^2\). AIC and BIC penalize additional complexity and can favor a simpler model. For predictive selection, cross-validation is also appropriate.
Different model families
For example, linear regression versus boosted decision tree (BDT) regression.		Out-of-sample MSE (minimize) or \(R^2\) (maximize), using the same validation observations or folds for both models.Directly compares predictive performance regardless of model architecture. AIC and BIC can also compare non-nested likelihood models when their likelihoods are comparable, but are not generally available in a comparable form for arbitrary learning algorithms.

See AIC and BIC and Adjusted R² for the definitions and derivations.

Practical workflow

  1. Reserve a test set for final evaluation; choose validation folds appropriate to the data (time-ordered for forecasting, grouped when observations share groups).
  2. Perform screening, feature selection, scaling and PCA within each training fold, never on the full dataset before validation.
  3. Compare candidate feature sets, model sizes and penalties using the chosen validation metric or comparable information criteria. Favor a simpler model when performance is similar.
  4. Refit the selected procedure on the available training data and evaluate once on the untouched test set.

For inference, ordinary p-values after selecting predictors on the same data need not remain valid. See Inference after Regularization.

Bayesian Regression

Model and Bayes' Rule

In Bayesian regression, we assign a prior distribution to the unknown coefficients and update it using the likelihood of the observed data. Instead of estimating a single set of coefficients, we obtain a posterior distribution over them.

\[\mathbf y=X\boldsymbol\beta+\boldsymbol\varepsilon,\qquad \boldsymbol\varepsilon\mid X\sim\mathcal N_n(\mathbf0,\sigma_\varepsilon^2 I_n).\]

With \(p\) predictors and an intercept, \(X\in\mathbb R^{n\times(p+1)}\), \(\boldsymbol\beta\in\mathbb R^{p+1}\), and \(\mathbf y\in\mathbb R^n\). First assume that the error variance \(\sigma_\varepsilon^2\) is known.

\[p(\boldsymbol\beta\mid X,\mathbf y)=\frac{p(\mathbf y\mid X,\boldsymbol\beta)\,p(\boldsymbol\beta)}{p(\mathbf y\mid X)}.\]
TermMeaning
Prior \(p(\boldsymbol\beta)\)Initial beliefs about the coefficients before observing the training data
Likelihood \(p(\mathbf y\mid X,\boldsymbol\beta)\)Density of the observed responses given the predictors and coefficients
Marginal likelihood \(p(\mathbf y\mid X)\)Normalizing constant obtained by integrating the likelihood times the prior over all coefficients
Posterior \(p(\boldsymbol\beta\mid X,\mathbf y)\)Updated distribution over the coefficients after observing the data

Gaussian prior and likelihood

Choose a zero-mean Gaussian prior with positive definite covariance \(\Sigma_p\):

\[\begin{aligned}\boldsymbol\beta&\sim\mathcal N_{p+1}(\mathbf0,\Sigma_p),\\p(\boldsymbol\beta)&=\frac{\exp\!\left(-\frac12\boldsymbol\beta^{\mathsf T}\Sigma_p^{-1}\boldsymbol\beta\right)}{(2\pi)^{(p+1)/2}|\Sigma_p|^{1/2}}.\end{aligned}\]

Conditional independence and Gaussian errors give the likelihood, as in Maximum Likelihood Estimation:

\[\begin{aligned}p(\mathbf y\mid X,\boldsymbol\beta)&=\prod_{i=1}^n\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma_\varepsilon^2}}\exp\!\left[-\frac{(y_i-\mathbf x_i^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\beta)^2}{2\sigma_\varepsilon^2}\right]\\&=(2\pi\sigma_\varepsilon^2)^{-n/2}\exp\!\left[-\frac{\|\mathbf y-X\boldsymbol\beta\|_2^2}{2\sigma_\varepsilon^2}\right].\end{aligned}\]

A Gaussian prior combined with this Gaussian likelihood yields a Gaussian posterior over the coefficients.

Posterior Distribution — Known Error Variance

Derivation by completing the square

Ignore factors that do not depend on \(\boldsymbol\beta\) and multiply the likelihood by the prior:

\[\begin{aligned}p(\boldsymbol\beta\mid X,\mathbf y)&\propto\exp\!\left[-\frac{(\mathbf y-X\boldsymbol\beta)^{\mathsf T}(\mathbf y-X\boldsymbol\beta)}{2\sigma_\varepsilon^2}\right]\exp\!\left[-\frac12\boldsymbol\beta^{\mathsf T}\Sigma_p^{-1}\boldsymbol\beta\right]\\&=\exp\!\left[-\frac{\mathbf y^{\mathsf T}\mathbf y-2\boldsymbol\beta^{\mathsf T}X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf y+\boldsymbol\beta^{\mathsf T}X^{\mathsf T}X\boldsymbol\beta}{2\sigma_\varepsilon^2}-\frac12\boldsymbol\beta^{\mathsf T}\Sigma_p^{-1}\boldsymbol\beta\right]\\&\propto\exp\!\left[-\frac12\boldsymbol\beta^{\mathsf T}A\boldsymbol\beta+\boldsymbol\beta^{\mathsf T}\mathbf b\right],\end{aligned}\]

where the precision matrix \(A\) and vector \(\mathbf b\) are

\[A=\frac{X^{\mathsf T}X}{\sigma_\varepsilon^2}+\Sigma_p^{-1},\qquad \mathbf b=\frac{X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf y}{\sigma_\varepsilon^2}.\]

Complete the square with \(\boldsymbol\mu=A^{-1}\mathbf b\):

\[\begin{aligned}-\frac12\boldsymbol\beta^{\mathsf T}A\boldsymbol\beta+\boldsymbol\beta^{\mathsf T}\mathbf b&=-\frac12(\boldsymbol\beta-A^{-1}\mathbf b)^{\mathsf T}A(\boldsymbol\beta-A^{-1}\mathbf b)+\frac12\mathbf b^{\mathsf T}A^{-1}\mathbf b\\p(\boldsymbol\beta\mid X,\mathbf y)&\propto\exp\!\left[-\frac12(\boldsymbol\beta-\boldsymbol\mu)^{\mathsf T}A(\boldsymbol\beta-\boldsymbol\mu)\right].\end{aligned}\]

Recognizing the multivariate Gaussian density gives:

\[\boxed{\boldsymbol\beta\mid X,\mathbf y\sim\mathcal N_{p+1}(\boldsymbol\mu,A^{-1})},\qquad \boldsymbol\mu=\frac1{\sigma_\varepsilon^2}A^{-1}X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf y.\]

The posterior mean combines information from the data and the prior; the posterior covariance quantifies the remaining uncertainty about the coefficients. With a Gaussian posterior, the mean is also the maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimate.

Connection to Ridge regression

For an isotropic prior \(\Sigma_p=\tau^2 I\), the posterior mean becomes

\[\boldsymbol\mu=\left(X^{\mathsf T}X+\frac{\sigma_\varepsilon^2}{\tau^2}I\right)^{-1}X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf y.\]

This is the Ridge estimator with \(\lambda=\sigma_\varepsilon^2/\tau^2\). Here all coefficients are penalized; to match ordinary Ridge with an unpenalized intercept, center the data and apply the prior to the slopes only.

Posterior Distribution — Unknown Error Variance

If the error variance is unknown, assign it an inverse-gamma prior and use a Gaussian prior on the coefficients conditional on the variance:

\[\sigma_\varepsilon^2\sim\operatorname{IG}(a_0,b_0),\qquad \boldsymbol\beta\mid\sigma_\varepsilon^2\sim\mathcal N_{p+1}(\boldsymbol\mu_0,\sigma_\varepsilon^2\Sigma_0).\]

Here \(\operatorname{IG}(a,b)\) has density proportional to \(s^{-a-1}\exp(-b/s)\) for \(s>0\). Use \(a_0,b_0>0\) and positive definite \(\Sigma_0\) for a proper prior.

Derivation of the joint posterior

Write \(s=\sigma_\varepsilon^2\). Multiply the likelihood, conditional coefficient prior and variance prior:

\[\begin{aligned}p(\boldsymbol\beta,s\mid X,\mathbf y)&\propto p(\mathbf y\mid X,\boldsymbol\beta,s)p(\boldsymbol\beta\mid s)p(s)\\&\propto s^{-n/2-(p+1)/2-a_0-1}\exp\!\left[-\frac{Q(\boldsymbol\beta)+2b_0}{2s}\right],\end{aligned}\]
\[\begin{aligned}Q(\boldsymbol\beta)&=(\mathbf y-X\boldsymbol\beta)^{\mathsf T}(\mathbf y-X\boldsymbol\beta)+(\boldsymbol\beta-\boldsymbol\mu_0)^{\mathsf T}\Sigma_0^{-1}(\boldsymbol\beta-\boldsymbol\mu_0)\\&=\boldsymbol\beta^{\mathsf T}A_0\boldsymbol\beta-2\mathbf b^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\beta+c,\end{aligned}\]
\[\begin{aligned}A_0&=X^{\mathsf T}X+\Sigma_0^{-1},\\\mathbf b&=X^{\mathsf T}\mathbf y+\Sigma_0^{-1}\boldsymbol\mu_0,\\c&=\mathbf y^{\mathsf T}\mathbf y+\boldsymbol\mu_0^{\mathsf T}\Sigma_0^{-1}\boldsymbol\mu_0.\end{aligned}\]

Complete the square with \(\boldsymbol\mu_n=A_0^{-1}\mathbf b\):

\[\begin{aligned}Q(\boldsymbol\beta)&=(\boldsymbol\beta-\boldsymbol\mu_n)^{\mathsf T}A_0(\boldsymbol\beta-\boldsymbol\mu_n)+c-\mathbf b^{\mathsf T}A_0^{-1}\mathbf b\\&=(\boldsymbol\beta-\boldsymbol\mu_n)^{\mathsf T}A_0(\boldsymbol\beta-\boldsymbol\mu_n)+S_n.\end{aligned}\]

Factor the joint posterior into a conditional Gaussian and an inverse-gamma density:

\[a_n=a_0+\frac n2,\qquad b_n=b_0+\frac{S_n}{2}.\]
\[\boxed{\boldsymbol\beta\mid s,X,\mathbf y\sim\mathcal N_{p+1}(\boldsymbol\mu_n,sA_0^{-1})},\qquad \boxed{s\mid X,\mathbf y\sim\operatorname{IG}(a_n,b_n)}.\]

Integrating out \(s\) gives a multivariate Student t posterior for \(\boldsymbol\beta\), with \(2a_n\) degrees of freedom, location \(\boldsymbol\mu_n\), and scale matrix \((b_n/a_n)A_0^{-1}\).

Setting \(a_0=b_0=0\), as in the supplied simplification, corresponds to an improper prior proportional to \(1/s\), not a constant. The conditional Gaussian formula still holds when the posterior is proper.

Making Predictions

Rather than choosing a single coefficient vector, Bayesian prediction averages over all possible coefficients, weighted by their posterior density. For a new input \(\mathbf x_*\) (including the intercept entry), define \(f_*=\mathbf x_*^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\beta\).

\[p(f_*\mid\mathbf x_*,X,\mathbf y)=\int p(f_*\mid\mathbf x_*,\boldsymbol\beta)\,p(\boldsymbol\beta\mid X,\mathbf y)\,d\boldsymbol\beta.\]

For known error variance, a linear combination of the Gaussian posterior coefficients is Gaussian. An independent new error contributes its variance to the prediction of an individual response:

\[\begin{aligned}f_*\mid\mathbf x_*,X,\mathbf y&\sim\mathcal N(\mathbf x_*^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\mu,\ \mathbf x_*^{\mathsf T}A^{-1}\mathbf x_*),\\y_*\mid\mathbf x_*,X,\mathbf y&\sim\mathcal N(\mathbf x_*^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\mu,\ \mathbf x_*^{\mathsf T}A^{-1}\mathbf x_*+\sigma_\varepsilon^2).\end{aligned}\]

As in Predictions, uncertainty in an individual observation includes both uncertainty about the fitted mean and irreducible error. With the inverse-gamma variance posterior, the corresponding predictive distributions are Student t, with \(2a_n\) degrees of freedom, location \(\mathbf x_*^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\mu_n\), and respective squared scales \((b_n/a_n)\mathbf x_*^{\mathsf T}A_0^{-1}\mathbf x_*\) and \((b_n/a_n)(1+\mathbf x_*^{\mathsf T}A_0^{-1}\mathbf x_*)\).

Feature Space and Kernel Trick

Transform the original inputs into a feature vector \(\boldsymbol\phi(\mathbf x)\) and apply linear regression in that space. For example, \(\boldsymbol\phi(x)=(1,x,x^2,x^3)^{\mathsf T}\) gives a cubic polynomial model.

\[f(\mathbf x)=\boldsymbol\phi(\mathbf x)^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\beta,\qquad \Phi=\begin{pmatrix}\boldsymbol\phi(\mathbf x_1)^{\mathsf T}\\\vdots\\\boldsymbol\phi(\mathbf x_n)^{\mathsf T}\end{pmatrix}.\]

With known error variance and zero-mean Gaussian prior, replace \(X\) with \(\Phi\) in the posterior formulas. Equivalently, define a kernel and its Gram matrix:

\[k(\mathbf x,\mathbf x')=\boldsymbol\phi(\mathbf x)^{\mathsf T}\Sigma_p\boldsymbol\phi(\mathbf x'),\qquad K=\Phi\Sigma_p\Phi^{\mathsf T}.\]

Let \(\mathbf k_*\) contain \(k(\mathbf x_i,\mathbf x_*)\). The predictive distribution of the latent function can be written directly using kernels:

\[\begin{aligned}\mathbb E[f_*\mid X,\mathbf y]&=\mathbf k_*^{\mathsf T}(K+\sigma_\varepsilon^2I_n)^{-1}\mathbf y,\\\operatorname{Var}(f_*\mid X,\mathbf y)&=k(\mathbf x_*,\mathbf x_*)-\mathbf k_*^{\mathsf T}(K+\sigma_\varepsilon^2I_n)^{-1}\mathbf k_*.\end{aligned}\]

The kernel trick avoids explicitly computing high-dimensional feature vectors when their inner products can be evaluated directly. This is the connection between Bayesian linear regression in feature space and Gaussian process regression.

Robust Standard Errors

OLS and the Sandwich Covariance Matrix

When errors have nonconstant variance or are serially correlated, the conventional OLS standard errors can be incorrect. Robust standard errors keep the OLS coefficient estimates unchanged but modify their estimated covariance matrix to obtain more reliable inference.

Let the conditional covariance matrix of the errors be \(\Omega=\operatorname{Cov}(\boldsymbol\varepsilon\mid X)\), with \(\Omega_{ij}=\operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon_i,\varepsilon_j\mid X)\). Under the classical error assumptions, \(\Omega=\sigma_\varepsilon^2 I_n\). In general, diagonal elements may differ (heteroskedasticity) and off-diagonal elements may be nonzero (correlated errors).

Derivation of the general OLS covariance

Start from the OLS coefficient estimator and its covariance, assuming full column rank:

\[\begin{aligned}\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}&=\boldsymbol\beta+(X^{\mathsf T}X)^{-1}X^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\varepsilon,\\\operatorname{Cov}(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\mid X)&=\operatorname{Cov}\left((X^{\mathsf T}X)^{-1}X^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol\varepsilon\mid X\right)\\&=(X^{\mathsf T}X)^{-1}X^{\mathsf T}\Omega X(X^{\mathsf T}X)^{-1}.\end{aligned}\]

With spherical errors, the expression reduces to

\[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{Cov}(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\mid X)&=\sigma_\varepsilon^2(X^{\mathsf T}X)^{-1}X^{\mathsf T}X(X^{\mathsf T}X)^{-1}\\&=\sigma_\varepsilon^2(X^{\mathsf T}X)^{-1}.\end{aligned}\]

Instead of assuming spherical errors, estimate the middle matrix \(B=X^{\mathsf T}\Omega X\). The resulting sandwich estimator is

\[\boxed{\widehat{\operatorname{Cov}}(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta})=(X^{\mathsf T}X)^{-1}\widehat B(X^{\mathsf T}X)^{-1}}.\]

The robust standard error of coefficient \(j\) is the square root of the corresponding diagonal element:

\[\widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\hat\beta_j)=\sqrt{\left[\widehat{\operatorname{Cov}}(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta})\right]_{jj}}.\]
Error structureMiddle matrix \(\widehat B\)When to use
Classical OLS\(s^2 X^{\mathsf T}X\)Constant variance and uncorrelated errors; \(s^2=\operatorname{RSS}/(n-p-1)\) with an intercept
HC0 (White)\(\displaystyle\sum_{t=1}^n e_t^2\mathbf x_t\mathbf x_t^{\mathsf T}\)Heteroskedasticity without serial dependence; HC3 is a common alternative with a leverage adjustment
HAC (Newey–West)Weighted sum of contemporaneous and lagged score productsHeteroskedasticity and serial correlation in ordered observations

Robust standard errors can be larger or smaller than classical standard errors. They do not correct biased coefficients due to endogeneity, improve the fitted values, or make OLS efficient. Unlike GLS, they do not change the fitting objective.

Newey–West HAC Estimator

Newey–West estimates standard errors that are heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation consistent (HAC). It extends the White estimator by including correlations between the regression scores at different time lags.

Let \(e_t=y_t-\mathbf x_t^{\mathsf T}\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\) be the OLS residual, \(\mathbf x_t\) the column vector of predictors (including the intercept), and \(\mathbf g_t=\mathbf x_t e_t\) the residual score. Define the unnormalized lagged cross-products:

\[\Gamma_\ell=\sum_{t=\ell+1}^n \mathbf g_t\mathbf g_{t-\ell}^{\mathsf T},\qquad \ell=0,1,\ldots,L.\]

Newey–West estimates the middle matrix using Bartlett weights \(w_\ell=1-\ell/(L+1)\), where \(L\) is the maximum lag:

\[\boxed{\widehat B_{\mathrm{NW}}=\Gamma_0+\sum_{\ell=1}^L\left(1-\frac{\ell}{L+1}\right)(\Gamma_\ell+\Gamma_\ell^{\mathsf T})}.\]
\[\widehat{\operatorname{Cov}}_{\mathrm{NW}}(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta})=(X^{\mathsf T}X)^{-1}\widehat B_{\mathrm{NW}}(X^{\mathsf T}X)^{-1}.\]

The zero-lag term accounts for heteroskedasticity, while the additional terms account for serial dependence. More distant lags receive smaller weights. With \(L=0\), this becomes HC0 (without finite-sample corrections).

HAC inference is asymptotic: it requires a consistent coefficient estimator and suitable weak-dependence and moment conditions. The resulting t-statistics and robust joint tests are not generally exact finite-sample Student t- and F-tests.

Using Newey–West in Practice

StepWhat to do
1. DiagnoseInspect ordered residuals and their autocorrelation function (ACF); check the Durbin–Watson statistic and other diagnostics.
2. Choose maximum lag \(L\)Use the sampling frequency, known overlap and persistence in the scores to guide the choice. A common initial rule of thumb is \(L=\lfloor4(n/100)^{2/9}\rfloor\); it is not a universal optimum.
3. Estimate HAC covarianceFit OLS on chronologically ordered observations with cov_type='HAC' and maxlags=L.
4. Read the resultsUse the updated standard errors, confidence intervals and p-values. Coefficients, fitted values and RSS remain unchanged.
5. Check sensitivityCompare plausible lag choices. Too few lags can miss dependence; too many can produce noisy covariance estimates.

Additional Comments

Categorical Predictors and Dummy Variables

Categorical predictors can be included in linear regression by creating binary indicators (dummy variables). For a categorical variable with \(K\) levels, use \(K-1\) dummies when an intercept is present. The omitted level is the reference category.

Including all \(K\) indicators together with an intercept creates perfect multicollinearity because their sum is always 1 (the dummy-variable trap). Without an intercept, all \(K\) indicators can be used for a single categorical predictor, provided the design remains full rank.

Example — three categories

Consider a response \(y\), a numerical predictor \(x\), and a categorical predictor with levels A, B and C. Choose A as the reference.

Category\(D_B\)\(D_C\)Conditional mean
A (reference)00\(\beta_0+\beta_1 x\)
B10\(\beta_0+\beta_1 x+\gamma_B\)
C01\(\beta_0+\beta_1 x+\gamma_C\)
\[y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i+\gamma_B D_{B,i}+\gamma_C D_{C,i}+\varepsilon_i.\]

Each dummy coefficient is the difference in expected response relative to A, holding \(x\) fixed. For example, \(\gamma_B=5\) means that category B has an expected response 5 units higher than A at the same \(x\).

To allow slopes to differ across categories, include interaction terms such as \(xD_B\) and \(xD_C\). Avoid encoding unordered categories as 0, 1, 2 directly, as this imposes an artificial order and equal spacing of effects. Fit the encoder on the training data and handle rare or unseen categories consistently.

See Model Assumptions — No Perfect Multicollinearity.

Why Not Linear Regression for Classification?

For a binary response \(Y\in\{0,1\}\), the conditional mean is a probability:

\[E[Y\mid x]=P(Y=1\mid x)=\pi(x).\]

OLS applied to a binary response is called a linear probability model. It can be useful for estimating approximate probability changes, but has several limitations for classification:

ProblemReasonConsequence
Unbounded predictions\(\hat y=x^T\hat\beta\) is not restricted to \([0,1]\).Predictions may be invalid probabilities.
Heteroskedasticity\(\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid x)=\pi(x)(1-\pi(x))\).Classical OLS standard errors are generally invalid.
Linear probability assumptionThe same change in probability per unit of a predictor is imposed everywhere.May poorly represent probabilities near 0 or 1.

Prefer logistic regression when the goal is to estimate binary class probabilities. It models the log-odds as a linear function of the predictors and uses the Bernoulli likelihood:

\[\log\frac{\pi(x)}{1-\pi(x)}=x^T\beta,\qquad \pi(x)=\frac{1}{1+\exp(-x^T\beta)}.\]

The predicted probabilities lie between 0 and 1. A class can then be assigned using a threshold selected according to the costs of false positives and false negatives. For more than two unordered classes, consider multinomial logistic regression.

Common Loss Functions

Let \(e_i=y_i-\hat y_i\). Training minimizes the sum of individual losses, \(\sum_{i=1}^n L(e_i)\). The loss function determines how different prediction errors are penalized and what aspect of the conditional response distribution is estimated.

LossIndividual loss \(L(e)\)When favorable / what to observe
Squared error (RSS / MSE)\(e^2\)Estimate the conditional mean; residuals have no severe outliers or heavy tails, or large errors are particularly costly. Gaussian noise gives the usual MLE interpretation.
Absolute error (MAE / LAD)\(|e|\)Estimate the conditional median; residuals exhibit heavy tails or unusually large errors that should not dominate the fit. Less sensitive to response outliers than squared loss.
Huber loss\(\displaystyle L_\delta(e)=\begin{cases}e^2/2,& |e|\le\delta\\ \delta(|e|-\delta/2),& |e|>\delta\end{cases}\)Most residuals are moderate but a minority are extreme. Quadratic near zero and linear in the tails; balances squared and absolute loss. Tune \(\delta\) using residual scale and validation.
Quantile (pinball) loss\(\displaystyle L_\tau(e)=\begin{cases}\tau e,&e\ge0\\(\tau-1)e,&e<0\end{cases}\)Estimate a conditional quantile, e.g. the 90th percentile for demand or risk. Useful for skewed distributions, varying uncertainty or unequal underprediction and overprediction costs. \(\tau=0.5\) is proportional to MAE.
Weighted squared error (WLS)\(w_i e_i^2\), \(w_i>0\)Residual plots show changing variance across observations. Use weights approximately inverse to the conditional error variance to improve efficiency when the variance model is reliable.

For binary classification, the standard loss associated with logistic regression is binary cross-entropy, \(-y\log\pi-(1-y)\log(1-\pi)\), derived from the Bernoulli likelihood.

MAE and Huber reduce sensitivity to large residuals, but do not automatically protect against high-leverage predictor outliers. Inspect those separately.

How to Choose a Loss Function in Practice

Start with a baseline OLS fit, inspect the residuals (preferably also on validation data), and decide whether the main objective is estimating the mean, the median, a quantile, or minimizing a particular business cost.

What to checkWhat to look forPotential action
Residuals vs fitted values / predictorsCurvature or systematic patternsImprove model specification, add nonlinear terms or interactions. Changing the loss alone does not correct a misspecified mean.
Residuals vs fitted valuesFanning or varying spreadConsider WLS or a suitable response transformation (e.g. log for positive responses). If inference is the only concern, consider robust standard errors instead.
Histogram and Q–Q plotHeavy tails or extreme residualsCheck whether they are genuine observations or errors; compare Huber and MAE against MSE.
Residual skew and prediction goalAsymmetric conditional distribution, or unequal costs of under- and overpredictionUse quantile loss when the relevant target is a quantile rather than the conditional mean.
Leverage and influenceExtreme predictor values or observations that strongly change the fitInvestigate data quality and sensitivity of the fitted model; robust loss alone may not be sufficient.
Residuals over time / ACFSerial dependenceModel the dependence or use appropriate time-based validation; HAC standard errors address inference, not the fitted mean.

Final selection: compare candidate losses using the same validation splits and the same evaluation metric aligned with the intended prediction goal. Training losses on different scales are not directly comparable. Tune loss-specific parameters on training/validation data, not the final test set.

See Diagnostics, Robust Standard Errors and Model Selection.

Bias–Variance Trade-off

MSE Decomposition

Prediction error can be divided into reducible error (bias and variance of the learned model) and irreducible error (random variation not explained by the available predictors).

Consider a fixed test input \(x_0\) and an independent new observation:

\[Y_0=f(x_0)+\varepsilon_0,\qquad \mathbb E[\varepsilon_0\mid x_0]=0,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_0\mid x_0)=\sigma_\varepsilon^2.\]

Here \(f(x_0)\) is the true conditional mean and \(\hat f(x_0)\) is the prediction from a model trained on a random training dataset \(\mathcal D\). The prediction varies across training datasets. Assume the new error is independent of the training data at fixed \(x_0\); all expectations below are at this fixed input.

Derivation from expected test MSE

Expand the squared prediction error:

\[\begin{aligned} \mathbb E[(Y_0-\hat f(x_0))^2] &=\mathbb E[(f(x_0)-\hat f(x_0)+\varepsilon_0)^2]\\ &=\mathbb E[(f(x_0)-\hat f(x_0))^2]\\ &\quad+2\mathbb E[(f(x_0)-\hat f(x_0))\varepsilon_0]+\mathbb E[\varepsilon_0^2]. \end{aligned}\]

The cross term vanishes by independence and zero mean, and the second moment of the noise equals its variance:

\[\begin{aligned} \mathbb E[(f(x_0)-\hat f(x_0))\varepsilon_0] &=\mathbb E[f(x_0)-\hat f(x_0)]\,\mathbb E[\varepsilon_0]=0,\\ \mathbb E[\varepsilon_0^2]&=\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_0)+(\mathbb E[\varepsilon_0])^2=\sigma_\varepsilon^2. \end{aligned}\]

Therefore,

\[\mathbb E[(Y_0-\hat f(x_0))^2]=\underbrace{\mathbb E[(f(x_0)-\hat f(x_0))^2]}_{\text{Reducible}}+\underbrace{\sigma_\varepsilon^2}_{\text{Irreducible}}.\]

To decompose the reducible error, let \(m=\mathbb E_{\mathcal D}[\hat f(x_0)]\). Add and subtract \(m\):

\[\begin{aligned} \mathbb E[(f(x_0)-\hat f(x_0))^2] &=\mathbb E[((f(x_0)-m)+(m-\hat f(x_0)))^2]\\ &=(f(x_0)-m)^2+\mathbb E[(m-\hat f(x_0))^2]\\ &\quad+2(f(x_0)-m)\mathbb E[m-\hat f(x_0)]\\ &=(f(x_0)-m)^2+\operatorname{Var}_{\mathcal D}(\hat f(x_0)), \end{aligned}\]

because \(\mathbb E[m-\hat f(x_0)]=m-m=0\). Define \(\operatorname{Bias}(\hat f(x_0))=m-f(x_0)\).

\[\boxed{\operatorname{MSE}_{\mathrm{test}}(x_0)=\underbrace{\operatorname{Bias}(\hat f(x_0))^2+\operatorname{Var}_{\mathcal D}(\hat f(x_0))}_{\text{Reducible error}}+\underbrace{\sigma_\varepsilon^2}_{\text{Irreducible error}}}\]
ComponentMeaningTypical effect of greater flexibility
Squared biasSystematic difference between the average learned prediction and the true conditional meanDecreases as the model captures more of the underlying relationship
VarianceVariability of the prediction across different training datasetsOften increases as the model becomes more sensitive to the training sample
Irreducible errorConditional variance of the new observation around the true meanUnchanged for the same predictors and data-generating process

The expected test MSE cannot be below the irreducible error. For heteroskedastic noise, replace \(\sigma_\varepsilon^2\) by \(\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_0\mid x_0)\). To obtain overall generalization error, average the pointwise decomposition over the test input distribution.

Multivariate parameter estimation

For a fixed parameter vector \(\boldsymbol\theta\) and its estimator \(\widehat{\boldsymbol\theta}\), the analogous squared Euclidean estimation error is

\[\mathbb E[\lVert\widehat{\boldsymbol\theta}-\boldsymbol\theta\rVert_2^2]=\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{Cov}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\theta}))+\lVert\mathbb E[\widehat{\boldsymbol\theta}]-\boldsymbol\theta\rVert_2^2.\]

This follows by summing the scalar bias–variance identities over the parameter coordinates. It is parameter estimation MSE, not test-response prediction MSE, so there is no additional test-noise term.

Model Complexity and Generalization

Increasing model flexibility typically reduces bias but increases variance. Initially bias may fall faster than variance rises, improving test MSE. Beyond a certain complexity, variance may dominate and test performance deteriorates.

ModelTypical behaviorTraining vs validation error
UnderfittingHigh bias, often low variance. Misses important patterns.Both errors high relative to a suitable benchmark
Appropriate fitCaptures the main structure without learning too much noise.Both errors reasonably low
OverfittingHigh variance, often low bias. Sensitive to noise and outliers.Low training error but high validation error

The best complexity depends on the true function, sample size and noise. A nearly linear relationship may need very little flexibility; a strongly nonlinear one may benefit from more. These curves describe a common pattern, not a universal law.

Flexibility vs interpretability: simpler models are often easier to interpret and more useful for inference; flexible models can improve prediction when they capture genuine structure. For nested OLS models, training MSE cannot increase as predictors are added, so training fit alone cannot select the best predictive complexity.

Learning Curves and Practical Remedies

A learning curve plots training and cross-validation error against the number of training observations. A validation curve plots those errors against a hyperparameter controlling complexity (e.g. polynomial degree, Ridge penalty or number of neighbors in KNN).

When both errors converge and plateau at a high level relative to a reasonable benchmark, more data alone is unlikely to solve the problem. A persistent large gap suggests overfitting and may shrink with more data. Variability across validation folds can indicate instability, but neither the fold spread nor training-error spread directly measures the theoretical bias or variance.

Reduce bias (underfitting)Reduce variance (overfitting)
Increase model flexibility (e.g. polynomial or interaction terms)Reduce complexity or select fewer features
Add informative features or improve model architecture using error analysisCollect more representative training data; improve data quality
Reduce excessive regularizationIncrease regularization; consider PCA or dropout where appropriate
Train longer or improve scaling if optimization has not convergedUse early stopping based on validation error
Consider boosting to improve a weak learnerConsider bagging or averaging models

Choose the model complexity and penalty using cross-validation, with feature selection and preprocessing performed inside each training fold. Use an untouched test set for final evaluation. For time-series data, preserve temporal ordering.
